entries.h: The stripper: what you give up without reflux
entries.x: In a stripping column the liquid feed itself is the only liquid in the column. The operating line runs from the bottoms composition, (x B , x B ), with slope L̄/V̄ greater than 1, and ends at the feed composition. The vapour leaving the top tray is the overhead product, so it can never be richer than the vapour that would be in equilibrium with the feed. More boil-up gives cleaner bottoms but a leaner, larger overhead. The minimum boil-up is set by a pinch at the top of the column (Example 4).

entries.h: The rectifier: what you give up without a reboiler
entries.x: In a rectifying column the vapour feed is the only vapour. The operating line runs from (x D , x D ) with slope L/V below 1, and the bottom liquid composition falls out of the balance. Pinch is at the bottom: the bottom liquid can approach, but not pass, equilibrium with the feed vapour. More reflux gives a richer distillate but sends more of the light component down with the bottoms (Example 5).

entries.h: Live steam instead of a reboiler
entries.x: When the heavy component is water, steam can be blown straight into the bottom of the column. You save the reboiler, its fouling and its corrosion, and you can strip at a lower bottom temperature. The cost is dilution: every kilogram of steam condensed ends up in the bottoms, so for the same bottoms mole fraction more of the light component is lost. On the McCabe–Thiele diagram the stripping line now ends at (x B , 0) instead of on the diagonal, because the vapour entering the bottom tray contains no light component. The overall balance gains a stream: F + S = D + B (Example 6). Rule of thumb. If only one product needs to be pure, ask whether a stripper or a rectifier will do before buying a second exchanger and its controls. Batch distillation is a rectifier on top of a still pot that acts as the reboiler. The pot composition falls with time, so reflux is raised or the cut is changed as the run goes on. 03

entries.h: Types of columns and where they are used
entries.x: Columns are classified in several overlapping ways: by operation (continuous or batch), by internals (trays or packing), by pressure (vacuum, atmospheric or pressure), and by how the separation is achieved when plain distillation is not enough. Continuous columns Steady feed and products; by far the most common. Design methods on this page assume steady state. Refineries, gas plants, petrochemicals, bulk chemicals. Batch columns A still pot, a rectifying column and a condenser. Flexible for many products and small volumes; compositions change with time. Pharmaceuticals, fine chemicals, solvent recovery, spirits. Trayed columns Discrete stages; easy to inspect and clean, tolerant of high liquid rates and fouling, suited to large diameters and side draws. Most pressure columns, fouling services, amine and sour-water units. Packed columns Random or structured packing; low pressure drop per stage, small hold-up. Usually the first choice under vacuum and in small diameters 33 . Vacuum and heat-sensitive service, revamps for capacity, corrosive service in plastics or ceramics. Vacuum columns Lower pressure lowers boiling points, which protects heat-sensitive products. Structured packing keeps the pressure drop, and hence the bottom temperature, low; it is used in columns making about 70 % of the world’s styrene monomer 36 . Crude vacuum units, styrene, fatty acids, fragrances. Superfractionators Close-boiling splits with α near 1. The propylene–propane splitter typically has 150 to 250 trays and a reflux-to-feed ratio of 5 to 10, and is often heat-pumped 23 . C₃ and C₂ splitters, xylene isomers. Crude and multi-draw fractionators One feed, many products drawn from the side, with pumparounds to remove heat and steam-stripped side strippers. The main column has no reboiler: heat comes from the fired heater and stripping steam. Atmospheric and vacuum crude units, FCC main fractionators. Extractive distillation A heavy solvent added near the top changes the relative volatility of the keys; the solvent leaves with the bottoms and is recovered in a second column. Aromatics recovery, ethanol dehydration with glycols, concentrating hydrochloric acid with sulfuric acid 22 . Azeotropic and pressure-swing distillation An entrainer forms a new, lower-boiling azeotrope that is decanted; or two columns at different pressures exploit an azeotrope that moves with pressure (section 05). Ethanol and isopropanol dehydration, acetic acid, HCl–water. Reactive distillation Reaction and separation in one shell; removing a product drives an equilibrium reaction forward. Ethers such as MTBE, esters such as methyl acetate. Dividing-wall columns A vertical wall turns one shell into a thermally coupled (Petlyuk) arrangement that makes three products with one reboiler and one condenser. Koch-Glitsch puts the potential savings at 20–30 % of capital and 20–50 % of energy against two conventional columns 24 . Chemicals (BASF built the first in 1985; hundreds now run), reformate splitting, NGL fractionation 24 . Heat-pumped columns The overhead vapour is compressed and condensed in the reboiler, so the condenser duty becomes the reboiler duty. Works best when the top-to-bottom temperature difference is small 23 . C₃ splitters, close-boiling alcohols. 04

Everything in a column design rests on the vapour–liquid equilibrium (VLE). If the equilibrium data are wrong near the product purity, no amount of careful hydraulics will rescue the design. At low to moderate pressure the modified Raoult’s law is the working relation: y i P = x i γ i P i sat (T) (3) ln P sat [kPa] = A − B / (T [°C] + C) (4) γ i is the liquid activity coefficient (1 for an ideal solution); equation (4) is the Antoine equation. Constants for common solvents are tabulated in thermodynamics texts 5 . Two calculations come up again and again. A bubble point finds the temperature at which a liquid of known composition starts to boil, and the composition of that first bubble: solve Σ x i γ i P i sat (T) = P for T. A dew point does the same for a vapour starting to condense: solve Σ y i P / (γ i P i sat ) = 1. The top tray of a column with a total condenser sits at the distillate’s bubble point; the reboiler sits at the bottoms’ bubble point.

The T–x–y diagram (Figure 3, left) has two curves at a fixed pressure. The lower one is the bubble-point curve, the upper one the dew-point curve. Below the bubble curve the mixture is all liquid, above the dew curve all vapour, and in between it splits into two phases. A horizontal tie line at any temperature joins a liquid composition x to the vapour composition y in equilibrium with it; the lever rule along that line gives the vapour fraction. The x–y diagram (Figure 3, right) plots y against x along with the 45° line. The further the curve bows away from the diagonal, the easier the split. This is the diagram McCabe–Thiele uses. Where it crosses the diagonal there is an azeotrope. Where to get VLE. Measured data (the DECHEMA collection, the NIST ThermoData Engine) first; then a fitted activity model (Wilson, NRTL, UNIQUAC) for polar liquids, or an equation of state (Peng–Robinson, SRK) for hydrocarbons and gases. Check any model against data at the product purities. Pressure and α. For most mixtures α rises as pressure falls, which is one reason C₃ splitters are run at the lowest pressure the heat sink allows 23 . Figure 3. The same equilibrium seen two ways: where the x–y curve crosses the diagonal, the T–x–y curves touch Mixture Pressure Liquid composition, x 1 – °C Bubble point of the liquid – Vapour in equilibrium, y 1 * – Relative volatility at x 1 , α – Azeotrope, mole fraction and temperature Temperature against composition, T–x–y Vapour against liquid composition, x–y Component 1 is the first-named. Modified Raoult’s law with Antoine constants 5 ; benzene–toluene ideal; methanol–water Wilson 5 ; ethanol–water and acetone–chloroform van Laar 4 . The activity-model parameters were fitted near 1 atm and are held constant here, so the shift of an azeotrope with pressure is indicative only. The van Laar model puts the ethanol–water azeotrope at 91.6 mol % against the measured 89.5 mol % (95.6 wt %) 19 ; models fitted over the whole range often miss the corner that matters most. 05

entries.h: Azeotropes and how to get past them
entries.x: An azeotrope is a mixture whose vapour has the same composition as its liquid. At that point y = x, α = 1, and boiling changes nothing, so ordinary distillation cannot cross it. On the McCabe–Thiele diagram the equilibrium curve meets the diagonal, and no reflux ratio can step past the meeting point. Try the “Ethanol near the azeotrope” preset in Figure 1 and push x D towards 0.92. Minimum-boiling (positive deviation, γ > 1). Unlike molecules repel each other, the mixture is more volatile than either component, and the azeotrope boils below both pure components. Ethanol–water at 101.3 kPa boils at 78.15 °C at about 95.6 wt % ethanol (4.4 wt % water), just below ethanol’s 78.3 °C 19 . Most azeotropes are of this kind. Maximum-boiling (negative deviation, γ < 1). Unlike molecules attract; the azeotrope boils above both components. Acetone–chloroform boils at 64.5 °C at an acetone mole fraction of about 0.34 21 ; hydrochloric acid has a constant-boiling mixture at 20.2 wt % HCl and 108.6 °C 22 . Heterogeneous azeotropes. The liquid splits into two phases at the azeotrope. Benzene–water boils at 69.3 °C, well below either component, and the condensate separates into a benzene-rich and a water-rich layer 20 . The two layers are the basis of decanter-assisted azeotropic distillation.

Azeotropic composition changes with pressure. For ethanol–water the water content rises from 4.4 wt % at 760 mmHg to 4.75 wt % at 1,451 mmHg, and the azeotrope disappears below roughly 75 mmHg 19 . That movement is small, which is why ethanol is not dried by pressure swing. Where an azeotrope moves a lot, two columns at different pressures can walk around it: one column makes pure A and an azeotrope at pressure p₁, the other takes that azeotrope at p₂, where it has a different composition, and makes pure B. HCl–water can be concentrated this way 22 .

entries.h: The usual ways round an azeotrope
entries.x: Method How it works Watch out for Pressure swing Two columns at two pressures, recycling the azeotrope between them Needs a large shift in azeotropic composition; large recycle; high-pressure column temperature Extractive distillation A high-boiling solvent fed near the top raises α of the keys and leaves with the bottoms Solvent selection, solvent recovery column, solvent losses and degradation Heterogeneous azeotropic distillation An entrainer forms a low-boiling heteroazeotrope; a decanter on the overhead splits it into two liquids Liquid–liquid split on the trays, multiple steady states, entrainer toxicity (benzene was used historically) Adsorption A molecular sieve takes up the minor component (water) past the azeotrope Regeneration energy and cycles; the adsorber is a separate unit Membranes and pervaporation A selective membrane removes one component across the azeotrope Flux, membrane life, fouling Salt or reaction A dissolved salt or a reacting agent shifts the equilibrium Solids handling, corrosion For three or more components with azeotropes, the tool is the residue curve map : the paths a liquid composition follows during simple boiling. Distillation boundaries on that map cannot be crossed by a single column, so the map tells you quickly which product sequences are possible before any simulation is run. Converting units. 95.6 wt % ethanol is (95.6/46.07) / (95.6/46.07 + 4.4/18.02) = 0.895 mole fraction. Keep mass and mole bases straight: VLE diagrams are almost always in mole fraction. Fuel ethanol. Plants typically take the beer-column vapour to a rectifier close to the azeotrope and finish the drying on molecular sieves, where pressure-swing adsorption takes over from distillation. 06

Before any stage is stepped off, close the balances. They fix the product flows, the internal liquid and vapour traffic (which sizes the diameter) and the condenser and reboiler duties (which size the exchangers and the utilities).

F = D + B (5) F z F = D x D + B x B → D = F (z F − x B ) / (x D − x B ) (6) The recovery of the light component in the distillate is D x D / (F z F ). For a multicomponent feed write equation (6) for every component and specify the split with two numbers, usually the recovery of the light key in the distillate and of the heavy key in the bottoms.

The feed’s thermal state decides how it splits between the two sections. q is the fraction of the feed that adds to the liquid flowing down below the feed tray: q = (H V − H F ) / (H V − H L ) ≈ 1 + c p,L (T bubble − T F ) / λ (subcooled) (7) q-line: y = [q / (q − 1)] x − z F / (q − 1) (8) Feed condition q Slope of the q-line Subcooled liquid > 1 Positive, steeper than the diagonal Saturated liquid (at its bubble point) 1 Vertical, x = z F Partly vaporised 0–1, the liquid fraction Negative Saturated vapour (at its dew point) 0 Horizontal, y = z F Superheated vapour < 0 Positive, shallower than the diagonal

With constant molal overflow (equal molar latent heats, negligible heat of mixing and heat loss), liquid and vapour flows are constant within each section: L = R D V = (R + 1) D L̄ = L + q F V̄ = V − (1 − q) F (9)

F h F + Q R = D h D + B h B + Q C (10) Q C ≈ V λ top Q R ≈ V̄ λ bottom (11) Equation (11) holds for a total condenser with saturated reflux and saturated products. Subcooled reflux adds to Q C and to the internal reflux. Equation (11) is why distillation is energy-hungry: every mole of distillate is boiled R + 1 times. Cutting R from 2.0 to 1.5 cuts the reboiler duty by about a sixth. It is also why the column, the condenser and the reboiler must be designed together: the diameter follows V and V̄, and so do the exchangers.

With open steam S (saturated, constant molal overflow) the stripping section has V̄ = S and L̄ = B, and the overall balances become: F + S = D + B F z F = D x D + B x B (12) Latent heats at the normal boiling point. Benzene 30.7 kJ/mol, toluene 33.2 kJ/mol, water 40.7 kJ/mol, methanol 35.2 kJ/mol. Equal molar latent heats are what make constant molal overflow a fair assumption for many organic pairs. When CMO fails. Large differences in molar latent heat or strong heats of mixing (ammonia–water, for example) need an enthalpy–composition (Ponchon–Savarit) method or a rigorous simulation. 07

McCabe–Thiele is a graphical solution of the stage-by-stage equilibrium and balance equations for a binary mixture with constant molal overflow. Simulators replaced it for design long ago, but it remains the best way to see what a column is doing, why it pinches and what reflux buys you. Figure 1 draws it for you; here is how to draw it by hand. Draw the equilibrium curve and the 45° line on an x–y diagram. Mark x B , z F and x D on the diagonal. Draw the q-line from (z F , z F ) with slope q/(q − 1). Draw the rectifying line from (x D , x D ) with slope L/V = R/(R + 1). Draw the stripping line from (x B , x B ) to the point where the rectifying line meets the q-line. Starting at (x D , x D ), step horizontally to the equilibrium curve (one equilibrium stage), then vertically to the operating line (the balance between stages). Switch to the stripping line on the first step that passes the intersection: that stage is the optimum feed stage. Stop when x ≤ x B . With a partial reboiler the last step is the reboiler; with a partial condenser the first step is the condenser. Rectifying line: y = [R / (R + 1)] x + x D / (R + 1) (13) Stripping line: y = (L̄ / V̄) x − (B / V̄) x B (14)

Minimum reflux. Lower R and the rectifying line swings down towards the equilibrium curve. When the operating lines first touch the curve, a pinch forms: the steps get infinitely small and the number of stages goes to infinity. For a well-behaved curve the pinch is at the feed; for curves with an inflection, such as ethanol–water, it can be a tangent pinch above the feed. For constant α and a saturated-liquid feed, Underwood’s equation gives R min directly: R min = [x D / z F − α (1 − x D ) / (1 − z F )] / (α − 1) (15) Total reflux. With no product withdrawn, both operating lines fall on the diagonal and the number of stages is the minimum. For constant α the Fenske equation gives it (stages include the reboiler): N min = ln{ [x D / (1 − x D )] · [(1 − x B ) / x B ] } / ln α (16)

entries.h: Operating lines when a section is missing
entries.x: Stripper (no reflux): y = s x − (s − 1) x B , s = L̄/V̄ = F/V̄, top point (z F , y D ) (17) Rectifier (no reboiler): y = s x + (1 − s) x D , s = R/(R+1), x B = [z F − (1 − s) x D ] / s (18) Live steam: y = (B / S) (x − x B ), which passes through (x B , 0) (19)

At high purity the steps near the ends become tiny. Redraw the ends on log scales, or use the Fenske or Kremser equations for that part of the column. A partial condenser is an equilibrium stage; a total condenser is not. Each side draw or second feed adds a new operating-line segment with its own slope. The method assumes constant pressure. A column with a large pressure drop (vacuum columns in particular) has a different equilibrium curve at the top and the bottom. Try it. In Figure 1, set the multiple of minimum reflux to 1.05 and watch the steps crowd around the feed: that is the pinch. Then set it to 3 and see how few stages are left. Feed on the wrong tray costs stages: the steps get smaller on one side. A real column usually has two or three alternative feed nozzles for that reason. 08

For multicomponent feeds the McCabe–Thiele picture no longer applies, but four classic equations give a quick design that is good enough to start a rigorous simulation and to check its answers 2 . Pick the light key (LK) and the heavy key (HK), specify their recoveries, and use α relative to the heavy key at an average column temperature.

entries.x: N min = ln[ (d LK / b LK ) (b HK / d HK ) ] / ln α LK,HK (20) d i / b i = (d HK / b HK ) · α i,HK N min (21)
Σ α i z i / (α i − θ) = 1 − q, with α HK < θ < α LK (22) R min + 1 = Σ α i x D,i / (α i − θ) (23)

entries.h: Gilliland: stages at a real reflux ratio
entries.x: Gilliland’s correlation links the two limits. Molokanov’s fit of it is convenient for calculation: Y = 1 − exp{ [(1 + 54.4 X) / (11 + 117.2 X)] · [(X − 1) / √X] } (24) X = (R − R min )/(R + 1) and Y = (N − N min )/(N + 1); N includes the reboiler.

entries.x: N R / N S = [ (B/D) (z HK / z LK ) (x LK,B / x HK,D )² ] 0.206 (25) Example 3 runs all four on a four-component feed. Figure 4 shows how well Gilliland’s correlation reproduces the stage counts from Figure 1 for a constant-α binary: the points stay close to the curve across the whole range of reflux. When the shortcuts mislead. Strongly non-ideal mixtures, azeotropes, large changes in α along the column, and wide-boiling feeds with large flow changes between sections. Use them to initialise a rigorous model (Aspen Plus RadFrac, HYSYS), never to replace it. Distributed non-keys. If a non-key has α between the keys or close to them, it splits between the products; equation (21) tells you how much. Figure 4. The black point is Example 3. 09

entries.h: From theoretical stages to real trays and packing
entries.x: Real trays do not reach equilibrium, and packing does not come in stages. Two numbers convert the theoretical answer into hardware: the overall tray efficiency for trays and the height equivalent to a theoretical plate (HETP) for packing. E o = N theoretical / N actual E MV = (y n − y n+1 ) / (y* n − y n+1 ) (26) E o is the overall (section) efficiency; E MV is the Murphree vapour efficiency of a single tray. For a first estimate, O’Connell’s 1946 correlation is still widely used. It needs only the relative volatility of the keys and the liquid viscosity in mPa·s, both at the average column temperature 9 : E o = 0.492 (α μ L ) −0.245 (27) Kister puts its accuracy at about ±25 % 6 , and its predictions tend to be conservative. Viscous liquids and high α both lower the efficiency. Field experience is the better guide when you have it: Field efficiencies as compiled by KLM Technology Group 35 . Absorbers and systems where one component is nearly insoluble run far below distillation values. Service, cross-flow trays Typical overall efficiency, % Propylene–propane splitter 85 Ethylbenzene–styrene 90 Debutaniser, depentaniser 80 Low-α aromatics 80 Alcohol–water 75 High-α aromatics 70 Amine contactor (absorber) 33 Hydrocarbon–water 15

Z = N theoretical × HETP (28) Kister’s rules of thumb for HETP in metres, for organic and hydrocarbon systems with surface tension below 25 mN/m and good industrial distribution, accurate to about ±25 % 6 : Metal random packings, 25 mm and larger: HETP = 93 / a p (29) Y-type structured packings: HETP = 100 / a p + 0.1 X-type (a p < 300): HETP = 145 / a p + 0.1 (30) a p is the packing’s specific surface area in m²/m³. For water-rich systems (surface tension near 70 mN/m) double the HETP; interpolate between. Vendors publish their own HETP curves and correlations, usually against the F-factor at several pressures; section 12 shows how to read them. Whatever the source, most designers add a margin to the stage count or the packed height, and the size of that margin should reflect how good the VLE data are. Why absorbers are less efficient. In an absorber the liquid-side resistance dominates and the stripping factor is far from 1, so each tray achieves a smaller fraction of equilibrium. Bed height. Liquid maldistribution grows with depth, so tall packed sections are split into beds with redistributors between them. 10

A cross-flow tray is a perforated deck with a weir at one end and a downcomer at each end. Liquid comes down the inlet downcomer, flows across the deck as a froth while vapour bubbles up through the openings, spills over the outlet weir and goes down the next downcomer. Figure 5 names the parts that appear on every tray data sheet. Figure 5. Anatomy of a single-pass cross-flow tray: vapour rises through the active area, liquid crosses it and falls through the downcomers Not to scale. Tray spacing 450–600 mm is typical; 600 mm lets a person crawl between trays through the manways in columns larger than about 1.5 m 33 . The downcomer clearance is set slightly below the outlet weir height so the downcomer stays sealed.

Sieve trays. A deck punched with holes; a common standard is a 2 mm deck with 12.7 mm holes and 10 % open area 10 . Cheapest and easy to clean, with low pressure drop, but they weep first as the vapour rate falls and have the narrowest operating range 11 . Moving (floating) valve trays. Developed in the 1950s: each hole has a cap held in a cage or by legs that lifts with the vapour rate and closes when it falls. Higher capacity than bubble caps and better turndown than sieve trays 11 . Valves can wear, stick or pop out in fouling or cyclic service. Fixed valve trays. Valves punched directly from the deck, introduced in the early 1990s; more capacity than moving valves, no moving parts, good in mildly fouling service 11 . Bubble-cap trays. A riser with a cap over it. Because there is no open hole in the deck, they cannot weep, which keeps them in use for very low liquid rates and wide-turndown services such as glycol contactors 11 . Lower capacity and higher pressure drop and cost. Dual-flow trays. No downcomers; liquid and vapour pass counter-currently through the same holes. Good in fouling and slurry service, narrow operating range. Baffle (shed, disc-and-donut) trays. Liquid curtains rather than froth; very fouling-resistant, low efficiency. Used in heavy-oil and slurry sections. High-capacity and high-performance trays. Multiple-downcomer trays, sloped or truncated downcomers, pushing valves that move liquid across the deck, and enhanced inlet areas. Vendor tests on one modern floating valve showed about 35 % more capacity than a traditional valve and twice the operating range before weeping 11 . Chimney trays. Collect all the liquid for a draw-off or a redistributor while vapour passes up through chimneys. Qualitative comparison after Kister 1 and the vendor review in 11 . Turndown is the ratio of maximum to minimum vapour rate with acceptable efficiency; real figures depend on the specific design and the liquid rate. Random packings are dumped into the column. First generation: Raschig rings and Berl saddles. Second: Pall rings and Intalox saddles, with windows that open up the surface. Third and later: shaped metal packings such as IMTP, Nutter rings and Raschig Super-Rings, with void fractions of 96–98 % 15 . Sizes run from about 15 to 90 mm: smaller means more efficient but lower capacity. Structured packings are stacked layers of corrugated sheet or gauze. Gauze packing (Sulzer BX, 1964) opened up fine vacuum distillation; corrugated sheet (Mellapak, 1976) became the general-purpose type 14 . Y-types have a 45° corrugation angle; X-types use about 60°, trading some efficiency for capacity. High-capacity versions smooth the flow at the joints between layers and add roughly 25–30 % capacity 14 . Grids are open, heavy-gauge structures with low surface area for fouling, wash and heat-transfer zones. Packing only performs if liquid and vapour reach it evenly, so the internals around it matter as much as the packing: liquid distributors and redistributors, feed devices for flashing feeds, collectors, support plates and hold-down grids. Maldistribution is the most frequent reason a packed column misses its HETP.

Favour packing when Favour trays when The column runs under vacuum or pressure drop must be low Liquid rates are high, or pressures are high and surface tension low The diameter is small, below about 0.6 m 33 , 37 The diameter is large and loads vary widely The service foams, or is corrosive and plastic or ceramic packing can be used The service fouls, cokes or polymerises and needs cleaning Liquid hold-up must be small (heat-sensitive products) Side draws, interreboilers or many feeds are needed A revamp needs more capacity or more stages in the same shell Pyrophoric scale is likely: trays are easier to clean and less prone to metal fires 26 Passes. When the liquid rate is high, the tray is split into two or four passes so each weir carries less liquid. More passes shorten the flow path and lower the efficiency slightly. Weeping and dumping. At low vapour rate liquid leaks through the deck openings (weeping); at very low rates all of it does (dumping) and the tray stops working. 11

The stage count fixes the height; the vapour and liquid traffic fixes the diameter. A tray works only inside a window. Push too much vapour and it floods; too much liquid and the downcomers back up or choke; too little vapour and it weeps or dumps. Sizing means placing the design point and the turndown point inside that window with margin.

Jet (entrainment) flood. Vapour carries so much liquid to the tray above that liquid accumulates and the column fills. The usual upper limit in low- to moderate-pressure columns. Downcomer backup flood. The liquid head needed to push liquid down the downcomer, against the tray pressure drop, rises until the froth in the downcomer reaches the tray above. Downcomer choke. The froth entering the downcomer is too fast to release its vapour. With high-pressure distillation and foaming systems this is the most common capacity limit 6 . Weeping and dumping. The lower limit: not enough vapour pressure drop to hold liquid on the deck. Spray regime. At low liquid loads the deck liquid is blown into spray. Weir loads below about 2–3 US gpm per inch of weir (18–27 m³/h per metre) can produce it 6 .

entries.h: Vendor data and how to read it
entries.x: The process engineer specifies loads and separation; the internals vendor designs the trays or packing and rates them. Most vendors give free rating software to customers, such as Koch-Glitsch’s KG-TOWER and Sulzer’s SULCOL 12 , 13 , and their outputs share a common layout. Knowing how to read them lets you check a proposal instead of taking it on trust.

A KG-TOWER-style tray report lists, for each section and each load case, three blocks 12 : Loadings : vapour mass rate, density, volumetric rate and viscosity; liquid mass rate, density, volumetric rate, surface tension and viscosity; the system factor. Geometry : tower diameter and area, number of passes, tray spacing, valve type and count (or hole diameter and percent hole area), downcomer widths and areas, weir height, downcomer clearance, active area, flow-path length. Results : jet flood %, downcomer flood %, downcomer backup, downcomer exit velocity, dry and total tray pressure drop, weir load and weir crest. The table below is such a sheet for the bottom tray of Example 7, produced with the correlations on this page. Read it from the bottom up: first the percentages of the three flood limits, then the weeping margin, then the pressure drop, and only then the geometry that gives those numbers. The design point and the minimum (turndown) point must both sit inside it. Figure 7 builds that diagram from the same correlations, so you can see how each geometry change moves each boundary. Packing vendors publish three kinds of curve, and each has a basis you must check before using it: Pressure drop against F-factor , one curve per liquid load. Koch-Glitsch’s IMTP curves, for example, are for air and water at ambient conditions in a 0.76 m (30 in) column, at liquid loads up to about 150 m³/(m²·h) 15 . Air–water data overstate pressure drop for organics, which wet better and foam less. HETP (or stages per metre) against F-factor , often one curve per pressure. Sulzer’s structured-packing curves are drawn for head pressures from 960 down to 50 mbar 14 . HETP is flat over the middle of the range and rises at both ends: at low F because of poor wetting, at high F because of entrainment and approach to flood. Capacity , as a maximum F-factor or a maximum efficient capacity. Sulzer quotes about 0.3–1.0 mbar per theoretical stage for Mellapak 250.Y, and 0.1–0.5 mbar per stage for BX gauze, which is why gauze is used for deep vacuum 14 . To use a curve, compute your superficial F-factor (F = u s √ρ V ), read the HETP at your pressure, correct it for your surface tension and viscosity if the vendor gives a correlation (Koch-Glitsch’s IMTP HETP correlation includes both 15 ), check the pressure drop per metre, and confirm the design F-factor is well below the maximum efficient capacity at both maximum and minimum rates.

What test system, pressure and column diameter is the curve or correlation based on? FRI data or the vendor’s own rig? Which flood definition and which system factor did you use? What is guaranteed: capacity, pressure drop, efficiency, or only the hydraulic rating? What is the turndown at the minimum case, and what limits it? For packing: distributor type, drip-point density, levelling tolerance and the expected HETP with that distributor. What installation and inspection tolerances apply, and who checks them? Different bases. Vendor capacity charts are often not on the same basis, which makes side-by-side comparison hard 11 . Put every option on your own loads before choosing. Low surface tension. At very high pressure, where σ falls towards a few mN/m, droplets are small and tray capacity drops faster than older correlations predict 16 . 13

The reboiler duty grows roughly in proportion to R + 1, while the number of stages falls steeply as R rises from the minimum and then flattens (Figures 1 and 4). The total annual cost therefore has a shallow minimum, usually somewhere between 1.1 and 1.5 times the minimum reflux 2 . When energy is expensive, the optimum moves towards the low end and the column gets taller.

Start from the condenser. Choose the lowest pressure at which the overhead can be condensed against the cheapest heat sink (cooling water or air) with a reasonable approach; refrigeration is expensive. Check the bottom. A higher pressure raises the bottom temperature; heat-sensitive or polymerising products set an upper limit, which may force vacuum. Check α. Most mixtures separate more easily at lower pressure, so the pressure choice trades condenser cost against column size and reboiler duty. Check the other side of every exchanger: the available steam or hot-oil temperature for the reboiler, and whether the condenser can heat another stream.

Feed preheat with the hot bottoms; a partly vaporised feed shifts duty from the reboiler to the feed preheater. Side reboilers and side condensers (pumparounds) move heat at less extreme temperatures, as crude columns do. Heat pumping for close boilers: compress the overhead and condense it in the reboiler 23 . Thermal coupling : dividing-wall columns for three-product splits 24 . Better internals : more stages in the same shell lower the reflux needed for the same split. Tight control : over-purifying a product wastes energy; controlling closer to specification saves it. Scale of the prize. Koch-Glitsch puts distillation at nearly 40 % of energy use in refining and chemical manufacturing 11 . A few percent off the reflux of a large column is worth real money and real emissions. 14

A two-product column with a total condenser has five valves that matter: reflux, distillate, bottoms, reboiler heat and condenser duty. The feed is usually set by the unit upstream. Three of the five must hold inventory, because column pressure, the reflux-drum level and the sump level do not regulate themselves. That leaves two for the two product compositions 38 . Most columns close one of those two with a tray temperature and leave the other on flow or ratio control 38 . Figure 8 draws that on a piping and instrumentation diagram (P&ID), the way a project would: every loop, each valve and how it fails, the alarms, and a separate layer of trips and relief.

Instrument tags follow ISA-5.1. The first letter is the measured variable: F flow, L level, P pressure, T temperature, A analysis, PD differential pressure. The letters after it say what the device does: T transmit, I indicate, C control, V valve, AHH alarm high-high 45 . All parts of one loop share its number, so FT-104 measures, FIC-104 controls and FV-104 moves. A plain circle is a field instrument. A circle in a square is a function in the basic process control system (BPCS). A diamond in a square is a safety instrumented system (SIS) function, the meaning ISA-5.1 now gives that symbol 44 . A line across the middle means the operator can reach it in the control room 45 . Dashed lines are electric signals. A line of small circles is a software link inside the control system: here, a cascade from one controller into a flow controller’s set point 45 . FC or FO beside a valve says whether it fails closed or open when it loses its air or signal. Why every valve has a flow loop. Each valve in Figure 8 is moved by a flow controller, even when the real target is a level or a temperature. The flow loop corrects changes in upstream and downstream pressure within seconds, so the outer loop works with a clean, nearly linear handle. Figure 8. entries.h: LV or DV: which stream holds the drum level
entries.x: The level loops decide which flows are left for composition, so they are the first real choice. In the standard LV scheme the distillate D holds the drum level and the bottoms B hold the sump, leaving reflux L and boil-up V for composition. In the DV scheme the reflux holds the drum level and the distillate rate is set directly, so a change in D changes the split at once. DV and LB are called material-balance schemes for that reason 38 . Two rules decide most cases. First, hold a level with the largest stream leaving the vessel; one common guide uses reflux for the drum level when L/D is above roughly 6 38 . A column at a reflux ratio of 15 cannot hold its drum level with a distillate valve that handles a sixteenth of the liquid. Second, the level tuning should not change the composition response. That favours LV: with DV, how the column responds to a change in boil-up depends on how the drum level is tuned 38 . Skogestad recommends LV with a fast temperature loop for most columns; the temperature loop also gives indirect level control, which makes LV workable for many high-reflux columns 38 . Switch Figure 8 between the two schemes and watch the cascades move.

A tray temperature is a cheap, fast stand-in for composition, but only on the right tray. The usual rules 38 , 39 : Put it where the temperature changes most from one tray to the next, and avoid flat parts of the profile. For a binary column the slope of the profile matches the gain of tray temperature to reflux closely 39 . Put it inside the column, not at the ends, where temperature hardly moves with composition. Put it at the end whose product matters most, usually the more valuable one. Close a stripping-section temperature with boil-up. Reflux reaches a bottom tray only after a delay, so it should not control a bottom temperature 38 . Correct it for pressure. A tray temperature moves with pressure as well as composition, so many systems control a pressure-compensated temperature. Luyben compared five criteria (slope, sensitivity, singular value decomposition, invariant temperature, and least change in product purity) on columns from ideal binary to azeotropic multicomponent. Singular value decomposition gave the most effective structure 40 , but the slope rule is the one most engineers try first. Install spare thermowells on a few trays either side of the chosen one; the best tray in operation is often not the one the simulation picked. An on-line analyser measures composition directly, but a gas chromatograph takes minutes per sample. Use it to trim the temperature set point slowly, not to move a valve. The names are confusing. Some texts call LV an energy-balance scheme, because L and V are the energy-related flows, and DV or LB material-balance schemes. Write on the P&ID which flow holds which level and the names stop mattering. Tune from the inside out. Flow loops first, then pressure, then levels, then the temperature. A tray temperature that moves with pressure will chase a poorly tuned pressure loop.

Pressure sets the temperature of every tray, so the pressure loop must be tight in the short term. Over the long term, running at the lowest pressure the condenser can hold usually raises relative volatility and saves energy 38 . The method follows from the condenser. Figure 8 shows the three that are most common with a total condenser. Column pressure control methods. The first three can be selected in Figure 8. Method What the valve does Use it for Watch for Condenser coolant Throttles cooling water, or moves fan pitch, fan speed or louvres on an air cooler. More cooling condenses more vapour and the pressure falls. Simple total condensers; the natural choice on air coolers Cooling water throttled to low velocity fouls, can freeze and responds slowly; one guide keeps the velocity above about 1 m/s and the outlet near 50 °C 43 . Air coolers swing with the weather. Flooded condenser Valve on the condensate line. Closing it backs liquid into the condenser; flooded tubes condense little, so the pressure rises 42 . Total condensers, with a small valve in liquid service Condensate should enter the drum below its liquid level 43 . Misreading the role of vapour pressure causes many of the problems with flooded-condenser schemes 42 . Hot-vapour bypass Valve in a line from the overhead to the drum vapour space; the condenser sits at grade, below the drum 41 . Closing it cools the drum surface, drains condensate from the condenser and exposes more tubes, so the pressure falls 43 . Large overheads where a valve in the vapour line would be huge; condensers kept at grade for maintenance Hot vapour heating the subcooled drum liquid upsets control; poor details have caused instability and even unit shutdowns 41 . Keep liquid pockets out of the bypass line 43 . Vent and inert gas Split range: nitrogen (or fuel gas) in over one half of the output, vent to flare over the other Overheads with inerts or light ends; columns near atmospheric pressure 43 Product lost to flare; inerts blanketing the condenser; nitrogen in the product Vapour product Valve on the vapour distillate of a partial condenser Partial condensers: deethanisers, stabilisers The drum level then needs its own handle, usually the condensation rate 43 Vacuum system Spillback or bleed at the ejector or vacuum-pump suction 43 Vacuum columns Air leaks that look like a control problem

Every control valve on the P&ID is given a position to go to when it loses air or signal, chosen so the column heads toward a cool, contained state. As a general rule, heating fails closed and cooling fails open 46 . On a column that usually means reboiler steam and feed fail closed and condenser coolant fails open. Product draws fail closed, so the column keeps its inventory and vapour cannot blow through an empty drum or sump into lower-pressure equipment. Reflux is often set to fail open, to keep the top trays wet while the heat input dies away. None of this is automatic: an open reflux valve can flood the top or empty the drum, so each position is confirmed in the HAZOP.

entries.h: The safety layer on the drawing
entries.x: The sienna symbols in Figure 8 are a separate system. Each trip has its own transmitter ( PT-116 , LT-112 , LT-115 ), its own logic in the SIS (interlock I-100 ) and its own final element: XV-117 and XV-121 in series with the control valves, and the pump motor starter. A trip that read PT-101 and closed FV-106 would fail together with the loop it is meant to back up, and could not count as an independent layer in a LOPA. Choose “Trips and relief” in Figure 8 to see this layer on its own. The cause-and-effect table states the trip logic in a form that operators and the HAZOP team can check line by line. For Figure 8: Cause-and-effect table for interlock I-100 in Figure 8 (illustrative). X means the action is taken. Trips latch and are reset by the operator once the cause has cleared. Each set point sits between the control-system alarm and the relief set pressure or the physical limit. HS-100 is in the control room and not drawn. In a published dynamic study of two industrial columns, a loss of cooling water took one column to its high-high pressure alarm in about 7 minutes and opened its relief valves within about 9. Pump-around reboilers kept adding heat, and the revised procedure gave operators 2 minutes after the alarm to isolate the column 47 . An alarm alone leaves the operator very little time; an automatic trip on every heat source is what keeps the relief valve shut.

Kister’s survey of 900 published malfunction case histories found plugging (of tray active areas, packing and distributors) at the top of the list, with coking, scale and corrosion, and precipitation as the usual causes. The tower base came second: liquid rising above the reboiler inlet caused premature flooding, internals damage and even tower overfilling 7 . Installation mishaps are also among the top five causes 31 . Flooding shows as a rising and erratic pressure drop on PDI-107 , worse separation, falling bottoms level and carry-over into the reflux drum. Foaming shows as flooding at loads well below the design, often after a contaminant arrives (hydrocarbons in amine, corrosion inhibitors, fines). Weeping and dumping show as a loss of efficiency at low rates, and sometimes as an unstable pressure drop. Damaged internals show as a step change in pressure drop or separation after an upset, a start-up or a pressure surge. A misbehaving control loop often looks like a process problem. Put the loop in manual: if the swings stop, the cause is tuning, a sticking valve or a bad measurement, not the column. Gamma scans locate flooding, missing trays, foaming and maldistribution without opening the column; temperature surveys and pressure-drop profiles narrow the search. Every opening of the column is a chance to inspect: levelness, weir heights, downcomer clearances, missing clamps and debris. Start-up. Columns are most vulnerable during start-up and shutdown: abnormal levels, water in hot oil, steam at the wrong place, and air reaching pyrophoric scale. Section 16 covers the safeguards. 15

No single code covers a distillation column. The shell is a pressure vessel, the overhead and reboiler lines are process piping, the condenser and reboiler are heat exchangers, the pumps are pumps, and the whole system needs overpressure protection and a process safety programme. The trays and packing themselves are designed to vendor standards and industry research (Fractionation Research Inc., FRI) rather than to a code. Owner and project standards (company engineering practices, PIP, NORSOK, IPS and the like) add to these; check which editions the contract invokes. Standard What it covers for a column system Pressure equipment ASME BPVC Section VIII, Division 1 (Division 2 for design by analysis) Shell, heads, nozzles, supports. UG-22 lists the loadings to design for, including wind, earthquake, the weight of contents and internals, and piping reactions; UG-27 internal pressure; UG-28 external pressure and vacuum; UG-99 hydrostatic test. Overpressure protection now sits in Section XIII 29 . ASME BPVC Sections II, V and IX Materials and allowable stresses, non-destructive examination, welding qualifications. CSA B51 (Canada) Registration of pressure-vessel and piping designs (the CRN) with the provincial authority, which in BC is Technical Safety BC 32 . ASCE 7 (US), National Building Code of Canada Wind and seismic loads on tall columns and their skirts and foundations. Piping, exchangers and machines ASME B31.3, ASME B16.5 and B16.47 Overhead, reflux, feed and reboiler piping; flanges. API Std 660, 661, 667 Shell-and-tube condensers and reboilers; air-cooled condensers; plate-and-frame exchangers. API 662 was withdrawn in February 2025; API 667 (2022) replaced its plate-and-frame part 48 . API Std 560 Fired heaters used as reboilers, as on the Texas City raffinate splitter. API Std 610 Centrifugal pumps for reflux and bottoms. Overpressure and safety API Std 521 Overpressure scenarios (loss of cooling, loss of reflux, power failure, blocked outlet, fire, abnormal heat input) and the relief and flare systems that receive them 28 . API Std 520, Parts I and II Sizing, selection and installation of relief devices 28 . IEC 61511 / ISA 84 Safety instrumented systems: high-pressure trips on the reboiler heat, independent high-level trips. API RP 752 and 753 Siting of permanent and portable occupied buildings near process units. CSA Z767 (Canada), OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (US) Process safety management: hazard analysis, operating procedures, management of change, mechanical integrity, pre-start-up reviews. CSA Z767:24 is the second edition 32 . Inspection API 510, API RP 572, API RP 580 and 581 In-service inspection, repair and rerating of pressure vessels; risk-based inspection planning.

For a column at modest pressure, internal pressure rarely sets the wall thickness. Wind and seismic bending on a tall, slender shell, external pressure, and the weight of a column full of water during the hydrotest usually do. The internal-pressure check for a cylindrical shell (ASME VIII-1, UG-27, circumferential stress) is still the first step: t = P R / (S E − 0.6 P) + c (41) P design pressure, R inside radius in the corroded condition, S allowable stress at design temperature, E joint efficiency, c corrosion allowance. Vacuum. Any column that is steamed out can be pulled into vacuum when the steam condenses, and many engineers design such columns for full vacuum as a matter of course; the extra cost is often just thicker stiffening rings 30 . If the column is not rated for vacuum, protect it with vacuum breakers and procedures, and never block it in after steaming. Hydrostatic head. The bottom of a tall column sees the design pressure plus the liquid head at relief conditions, and the hydrotest adds the full water head. Tray supports and uplift. Trays sit on rings welded to the shell and are clamped down. Specify an uplift rating where pressure surges are possible: water entering a hot column, rapid depressuring, or steam introduced too fast at start-up. Levelness. An out-of-level tray has an uneven liquid depth and loses efficiency and capacity. A typical acceptance limit is 3 mm out-of-level for columns up to 2 m diameter and 6 mm above 31 ; check the support rings at the fabrication shop, before the trays go in 31 . Base and sump. The reboiler return must stay above the highest liquid level, with room for surge; Kister’s survey ranks tower-base problems second only to plugging 7 . Fit vortex breakers on bottoms outlets and specify independent level instruments. Skirt and fireproofing. A pool fire under a column can weaken an unprotected skirt and bring the whole tower down; fireproof skirts and supports in fire zones. Manways. Usually one every 10 to 20 trays, plus at feeds, draws and the bottom; the trays below a manway need removable panels that pass through it. Materials. Carbon steel with a corrosion allowance for most hydrocarbon shells; stainless or higher alloys for trays and packing, where there is no allowance to spend. 16

A column holds a large flammable inventory near its boiling point, with a heat source at the bottom and a heat sink at the top. Most of its serious hazards come from losing the balance between the two, from losing track of where the liquid is, or from what happens when the column is opened.

entries.h: Overpressure: the scenarios API 521 asks about
entries.x: API 521 gives no credit for control action that would reduce the load; credit can be taken for a reboiler “pinch” as the column temperature rises at relieving pressure 27 . The unbalanced-heat method can be either conservative or not: in one published depropaniser study the dynamic relief load was about 13 % higher than the unbalanced-heat value 27 . Scenario What happens in the column Screening relief load Loss of overhead cooling (cooling water, fans, louvres) Vapour is no longer condensed; the reboiler keeps boiling; the reflux drum empties and reflux is lost Often the largest case: reboiler duty ÷ latent heat at relieving conditions 27 Loss of reflux (pump trip, valve closed) The top heats up, light material goes down, condenser load changes Unbalanced heat; usually smaller than loss of cooling, but check 27 Reboiler heat-input control fails open Duty rises to the maximum the heating medium can deliver Excess duty ÷ latent heat Blocked vapour outlet; condenser flooded with liquid Vapour has nowhere to go Full vapour generation Total or partial power failure Pumps and fans stop together; feed may stop; compositions shift Combine the failures; dynamic simulation often justifies a different load 27 External pool fire Heat input to the wetted shell Q = 43,200 F A w 0.82 W, with adequate drainage and firefighting 28 Abnormal heat input or rapid vaporisation Water or light material entering a hot column; reboiler tube rupture Case-specific; can also damage trays Overfilling Liquid reaches the overhead line and the relief valves Liquid or two-phase relief; prevent it instead

On 23 March 2005, during the start-up of the isomerisation unit at BP’s Texas City refinery, operators filled the raffinate splitter, a distillation column roughly 50 m tall, for about three hours without taking any liquid out. The level rose to about 15 times its normal value, the contents were overheated, the relief valves opened, and liquid hydrocarbon went to a blowdown drum and stack that vented to atmosphere. The vapour cloud ignited, killing 15 people and injuring 180 25 . The CSB found that the level transmitter and the high-level alarm were not working properly and misled the operators, that start-up procedures were not followed, and that 13 of the previous 16 start-ups had shown excessive levels without being investigated 25 . Afterwards BP said it would eliminate blowdown stacks venting directly to atmosphere at its US refineries 25 . Measure tower level with two independent instruments, compare them, and alarm on disagreement; make the high-high level trip independent of the control transmitter. Treat start-up and shutdown as the hazardous operations they are: written procedures, experienced supervision, instruments checked before feed is introduced. Relieve flammable materials to a closed flare system, not to an atmospheric vent. Site occupied buildings and trailers out of reach of a credible vapour-cloud explosion (API RP 752 and 753). Investigate near misses such as abnormal levels and pressures; they are the warnings.

Corrosion of carbon steel by hydrogen sulfide forms iron sulfide, which settles on packing and ignites in air at ambient temperature. Structured packing is especially exposed: it is made of thin sheet (0.1–0.2 mm) with a huge surface, and once lit it burns as a metal fire 26 . One operator reported that all of its packed-column fires had occurred in structured beds, none in random ones 26 . On 26 May 2020, during a turnaround at ENEOS’s Oita refinery, a fire in the structured packing of a 6.2 m diameter, 50 m tall crude column brought the column down about 70 minutes after the temperature rise was noticed 26 . Before opening, wash with an oxidising chemical (potassium permanganate is common) to passivate iron sulfide; steaming and water washing alone do not remove it 26 . Keep beds wet, monitor bed temperatures while manways are open, and have water ready to spray the packing 26 . Do not allow hot work above or below packing; new packing carries a film of lubricating oil that can burn too 26 . In fouling, sour services such as sour-water strippers, consider trays, which are easier to clean and less prone to metal fires 26 .

entries.h: Other hazards to cover in the HAZOP
entries.x: Deviation Typical causes Typical safeguards Less pressure, vacuum Steam-out followed by cooling or water wash; over-condensing; loss of heat while still condensing Full-vacuum design, vacuum breaker, procedures that keep vents open More temperature in the bottoms Lost reflux, high heat input, fouling; polymerisation or decomposition of heat-sensitive bottoms Vacuum operation, inhibitors, high-temperature alarms and trips, short residence time Other than: water into a hot column Wet feed, steam condensate, a leaking exchanger Drained feed lines, slow warm-up, uplift-rated trays Less level in the sump Bottoms pump runs dry; hot liquid lost to downstream Low-level trip on the bottoms pump, minimum-flow protection Toxic or flammable release Flange leaks, sampling, drains; H₂S in sour services; benzene Closed sampling, gas detection, leak-tight design, personal protection Entry and maintenance Confined space, toxic or inert atmosphere, falls inside a tall column Isolation by blinds, gas testing, entry permits, rescue plan All of this belongs in a process safety management system: hazard analysis at each design stage, operating procedures, training, management of change, mechanical integrity and pre-start-up reviews. In Canada, CSA Z767 sets these out as a 16-element system 32 . Inherently safer first. Less inventory (packing holds less liquid than trays), lower temperature (vacuum), less hazardous solvents (no benzene as an entrainer), and designs that cannot overpressure (a heating medium too cool to exceed the design pressure) beat added protection. Layers of protection. Basic control, alarms with operator response, an independent safety instrumented function, the relief valve, and the flare: each needs to be independent of the others to count. 17

Examples 1, 2 and 7 to 10 follow one column through from balance to relief valve: a benzene–toluene splitter at atmospheric pressure. Examples 3 to 6 cover the multicomponent shortcut and the three configurations without a full set of reflux and reboiler. Load the matching preset in Figure 1 to see each diagram.

entries.h: Example 1. Product flows, recoveries and section traffic
entries.x: Feed 100 kmol/h, 40 mol % benzene in toluene, saturated liquid (q = 1) Specification Distillate 95 mol % benzene, bottoms 5 mol % benzene Reflux ratio R = 1.878 (from Example 2) Distillate and bottoms from equations (5) and (6): D = 100 × (0.40 − 0.05)/(0.95 − 0.05) = 38.89 kmol/h; B = 61.11 kmol/h Recoveries: benzene to distillate = 38.89 × 0.95 / 40 = 92.4 % toluene to bottoms = 61.11 × 0.95 / 60 = 96.8 % Section flows from equation (9): L = 1.878 × 38.89 = 73.0 V = 2.878 × 38.89 = 111.9 L̄ = 73.0 + 100 = 173.0 V̄ = 111.9 kmol/h Two purities fix two flows. If the client asks for 99 % recovery as well as 95 % purity, one of those specifications has to give: the balance has no more degrees of freedom.

entries.h: Example 2. Minimum reflux, minimum stages and the McCabe–Thiele count
entries.x: Same column. Raoult’s law gives α between 2.37 at the bottom and 2.60 at the top for benzene–toluene at 101.3 kPa, so take a constant α = 2.5. Design at R = 1.3 R min . Minimum reflux, equation (15): R_min = [0.95/0.40 − 2.5 × 0.05/0.60] / (2.5 − 1) = (2.375 − 0.208)/1.5 = 1.444 R = 1.3 × 1.444 = 1.878 Minimum stages, equation (16): N_min = ln[(0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05)] / ln 2.5 = ln 361 / 0.916 = 6.43 (incl. reboiler) Step off the stages (Figure 1, Example 2 preset). Rectifying line y = 0.6525 x + 0.3301; the q-line is vertical at x = 0.40. The first steps run: stage 1: y = 0.950 → x = 0.884 stage 2: y = 0.907 → x = 0.796 stage 3: y = 0.849 → x = 0.693 … stage 7: y = 0.613 → x = 0.388 (crosses 0.40: feed stage) stage 14: y = 0.064 → x = 0.027 (passes x_B; reboiler) Count, with the last step fractional: N = 13 + (0.059 − 0.050)/(0.059 − 0.027) = 13.3 stages incl. reboiler, feed on stage 7 Cross-check with Gilliland, equation (24): X = (1.878 − 1.444)/2.878 = 0.151 → Y = 0.505 → N = (6.43 + 0.505)/(1 − 0.505) = 14.0 The shortcut lands within one stage of the stepped answer. With the full Raoult’s-law curve instead of constant α, Figure 1 gives R min = 1.47 and 13.6 stages: close, because benzene–toluene is nearly ideal.

entries.h: Example 3. A four-component column by Fenske–Underwood–Gilliland–Kirkbride
entries.x: Feed 100 kmol/h saturated liquid: A 10 %, B 40 %, C 35 %, D 15 % (mole) Volatilities α relative to C: A 4.0, B 2.0, C 1.0, D 0.5 (assumed constant, illustrative) Keys Light key B, heavy key C; 98 % of B to the distillate, 97 % of C to the bottoms Design R = 1.3 R min Key splits: d_B = 39.20 b_B = 0.80 d_C = 1.05 b_C = 33.95 kmol/h Fenske, equation (20): N_min = ln[(39.20/0.80)(33.95/1.05)] / ln 2 = ln(1,584) / 0.693 = 10.63 Non-keys, equation (21): A and D do not distribute. A: d/b = (1.05/33.95) × 4^10.63 ≈ 7.8 × 10⁴ → all 10 kmol/h to D D: d/b = (1.05/33.95) × 0.5^10.63 ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁵ → all 15 kmol/h to B D = 50.25 kmol/h, B = 49.75 kmol/h Underwood, equation (22), q = 1, solve for θ between 1 and 2: 4(0.10)/(4 − θ) + 2(0.40)/(2 − θ) + 1(0.35)/(1 − θ) + 0.5(0.15)/(0.5 − θ) = 0 → θ = 1.2947 Minimum reflux, equation (23), with distillate mole fractions A 0.199, B 0.780, C 0.021: R_min + 1 = 4(0.199)/2.705 + 2(0.780)/0.705 + 1(0.021)/(−0.295) = 2.435 → R_min = 1.435 R = 1.3 × 1.435 = 1.866 Gilliland, equation (24): X = (1.866 − 1.435)/2.866 = 0.150 → Y = 0.505 → N = (10.63 + 0.505)/(1 − 0.505) = 22.5 Kirkbride, equation (25), with x B,LK = 0.80/49.75 = 0.0161 and x D,HK = 1.05/50.25 = 0.0209: N_R/N_S = [(49.75/50.25)(0.35/0.40)(0.0161/0.0209)²]^0.206 = 0.872 N_R = 10.5, N_S = 12.0 → feed on about stage 11 from the top About 22 to 23 theoretical stages including the reboiler, R ≈ 1.87, feed near the middle. This is the starting point for a rigorous simulation, which will move the answer by a stage or two once α varies along the column.

entries.h: Example 4. A stripping column without reflux
entries.x: Feed Saturated liquid, z F = 0.30, fed to the top tray; α = 4 (constant) Specification Bottoms x B = 0.01; reboiler, no condenser Design Boil-up 1.5 times the minimum The pinch is at the top. The richest overhead possible is in equilibrium with the feed: y*(0.30) = 4(0.30)/(1 + 3 × 0.30) = 0.632 The steepest allowed operating line joins (0.01, 0.01) to (0.30, 0.632). Its slope is L̄/V̄ = F/V̄: s_max = (0.632 − 0.01)/(0.30 − 0.01) = 2.143 → (V̄/F)_min = 1/2.143 = 0.467 Design boil-up and overhead composition, from the balance: V̄/F = D/F = 1.5 × 0.467 = 0.700 y_D = [0.30 − (1 − 0.700)(0.01)] / 0.700 = 0.424 Step down from (0.30, 0.424) with y = 1.429 x − 0.0043: stage 1: y = 0.424 → x = 0.156 stage 2: y = 0.218 → x = 0.065 stage 3: y = 0.089 → x = 0.024 stage 4: y = 0.030 → x = 0.008 (reboiler) → 3.85 stages Three trays and a reboiler clean the bottoms to 1 % and recover 99 % of the light component, but the overhead is only 42 % light, and could never exceed 63 % however tall the column. If the overhead must be pure, add a condenser and reflux.

entries.h: Example 5. A rectifying column without a reboiler
entries.x: Feed 100 kmol/h saturated vapour, z F = 0.50, under the bottom tray; α = 2.5 Specification Distillate x D = 0.95; total condenser, no reboiler Design R = 1.5 R min The pinch is at the bottom. The leanest bottom liquid possible is in equilibrium with the feed vapour: x*(0.50) = 0.50/(2.5 − 1.5 × 0.50) = 0.286 Minimum reflux from the line through (0.95, 0.95) and (0.286, 0.50): (L/V)_min = (0.95 − 0.50)/(0.95 − 0.286) = 0.677 → R_min = 0.677/0.323 = 2.10 At R = 3.15, L/V = 0.759 and the bottom liquid follows from equation (18): x_B = [0.50 − (1 − 0.759)(0.95)] / 0.759 = 0.357 Balance: with no reboiler, V = F = 100 kmol/h: D = 100 / 4.15 = 24.1 kmol/h; B = L = 75.9 kmol/h check: 24.1 × 0.95 + 75.9 × 0.357 = 50.0 ✓ Stepping from the top (Figure 1, Example 5 preset) gives 5.4 theoretical stages. The rectifier makes 95 % product but recovers only 46 % of the light component; the rest leaves in a bottoms stream that can be no leaner than 28.6 %. That is why a rectifier is usually paired with a stripper that takes its bottoms, as in an ethanol plant’s beer column and rectifier.

entries.h: Example 6. Live steam or a reboiler for methanol–water?
entries.x: Feed 100 kmol/h, 30 mol % methanol in water, saturated liquid, 101.3 kPa Specification x D = 0.95, x B = 0.01; R = 1.3 R min VLE Wilson model (Figure 1, methanol–water); R min = 0.79, so R = 1.03 With a reboiler: D = 100(0.30 − 0.01)/(0.95 − 0.01) = 30.85; B = 69.15 kmol/h V̄ = 62.7 kmol/h stages: 10.9 incl. reboiler (9.9 trays + reboiler), feed on stage 7 methanol lost in bottoms = 69.15 × 0.01 = 0.69 kmol/h (2.3 % of feed methanol) With live steam, from equation (12) and L̄ = B, V̄ = S: D = F (z_F − q x_B)/(x_D + R x_B) = 100(0.29)/(0.95 + 1.03 × 0.01) = 30.20 S = (R + 1) D = 61.3 kmol/h (1,105 kg/h of steam) B = R D + F = 131.1 kmol/h stages: 10.8 trays, feed on stage 7 methanol lost = 131.1 × 0.01 = 1.31 kmol/h (4.4 % of feed methanol) To lose no more methanol than the reboiled column, the steam column must reach x B = 0.0053, which takes 11.4 trays. Live steam saves the reboiler at the cost of about one and a half extra trays and nearly twice the bottoms flow to treat. It pays where a reboiler would foul or corrode, or where the bottoms go to a water treatment plant anyway.

entries.h: Example 7. Column diameter at the top and the bottom
entries.x: Column Examples 1 and 2; sieve trays, 600 mm spacing, downcomers 12 % of the area, design at 80 % of flood Top 101.3 kPa, about 82 °C; vapour M = 78.8 kg/kmol; ρ L = 815 kg/m³, σ = 21 mN/m Bottom About 125 kPa after the tray pressure drop, 116 °C; M = 91.4 kg/kmol; ρ L = 775 kg/m³, σ = 17.5 mN/m Top section, mass flows and vapour density: V = 111.9 × 78.8 = 8,820 kg/h; L = 73.0 × 78.8 = 5,755 kg/h ρ_V = PM/RT = 101.3 × 78.8 / (8.314 × 355) = 2.71 kg/m³ Flow parameter and capacity, equations (31)–(33): F_LV = (5,755/8,820) √(2.71/815) = 0.0376 C_SB = 0.0105 + 8.127e-4 × 600^0.755 × exp(−1.463 × 0.0376^0.842) = 0.1032 m/s u_nf = 0.1032 × (21/20)^0.2 × √((815 − 2.71)/2.71) = 1.80 m/s Diameter, equation (34): Q_V = 8,820/3,600/2.71 = 0.903 m³/s; u_n = 0.8 × 1.80 = 1.44 m/s A_n = 0.626 m²; A_c = 0.626/0.88 = 0.711 m²; D = 0.95 m Bottom section, the same way: V̄ = 111.9 × 91.4 = 10,233 kg/h; L̄ = 173.0 × 91.4 = 15,821 kg/h ρ_V = 3.53 kg/m³ F_LV = 0.104; C = 0.0923 × (17.5/20)^0.2 = 0.0898 m/s; u_nf = 1.33 m/s Q_V = 0.804 m³/s; A_n = 0.757 m²; A_c = 0.861 m²; D = 1.05 m Rounding up to the next 50 mm gives 1.05 m at 80 % of flood. I would take 1.10 m for margin and use it for the whole column; at that diameter the top runs at 60 % of flood and the bottom at 72 %. The bottom governs here, because the liquid load below the feed raises the flow parameter. Figure 6 has both cases as presets; Figure 7 rates the bottom tray in full and shows it inside its window.

entries.h: Example 8. Real trays, column height and a packed alternative
entries.x: Efficiency by O’Connell, equation (27), with α = 2.45 and μ L ≈ 0.27 mPa·s at the average temperature: E_o = 0.492 × (2.45 × 0.27)^−0.245 = 0.544 Actual trays: 13.3 theoretical stages less the reboiler = 12.3 theoretical trays. N_actual = 12.3 / 0.544 = 22.6 → 23 trays Height, equation (39), with 1.5 m above the top tray, 2.5 m below the bottom tray and 0.3 m extra at the feed: H = (23 − 1) × 0.6 + 1.5 + 2.5 + 0.3 = 17.5 m tangent to tangent Packed alternative with a Y-type structured packing of 250 m²/m³, equation (30): HETP = 100/250 + 0.1 = 0.50 m; Z = 12.3 × 0.50 = 6.2 m of packing O’Connell is conservative for this service: field efficiencies near 80 % are reported for low-α aromatics 35 , which would give 16 trays. The packed column is much shorter and its pressure drop is a few millibar against about 250 mbar for 23 trays, which matters only if the column runs under vacuum or the bottoms are heat-sensitive.

entries.h: Example 9. Condenser and reboiler duties and utilities
entries.x: Condenser, total, saturated reflux, equation (11), with λ benzene = 30.7 MJ/kmol: Q_C = 111.9 × 30.72 / 3,600 = 0.955 MW Cooling water for a 10 K rise: m = 955 / (4.18 × 10) = 22.8 kg/s ≈ 82 m³/h Reboiler, with λ toluene = 33.2 MJ/kmol: Q_R = 111.9 × 33.18 / 3,600 = 1.03 MW Steam at 5 bar a (latent heat about 2,108 kJ/kg): m_steam = 1,031 / 2,108 × 3,600 = 1,760 kg/h Every 0.1 off the reflux ratio saves 38.9 × 0.1 = 3.9 kmol/h of boil-up, about 36 kW at the reboiler. Over a year that adds up quickly, which is why reflux is worth optimising and why over-purifying a product is waste.

entries.h: Example 10. A relief load and a shell thickness
entries.x: Loss of overhead cooling, unbalanced-heat screening: the reboiler keeps delivering 1.03 MW and nothing is condensed. Take the latent heat of the benzene-rich overhead at relieving pressure as about 350 kJ/kg (lower than the 393 kJ/kg at 1 atm): W = 1,031 kW / 350 kJ/kg × 3,600 = 10,600 kg/h of vapour Shell for internal pressure, equation (41): design 0.35 MPa gauge, D = 1,100 mm, SA-516 Grade 70 at S = 138 MPa, spot radiography E = 0.85, c = 3 mm: R = 550 + 3 = 553 mm t = 0.35 × 553 / (138 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 0.35) + 3 = 1.65 + 3 = 4.7 mm Pressure needs less than 5 mm here. Full vacuum (UG-28), wind on an 18 m column and the water-filled hydrotest will set the real thickness and the stiffening. The relief valve is then sized for 10,600 kg/h to API 520, unless a dynamic study with the credits API 521 allows supports a different load. 18
Try each one before opening the solution. Answers within 2 % count as correct unless stated. Several can be checked in Figures 1, 6, 7 and 8.

A column takes 250 kmol/h of a feed with 35 mol % light component. The distillate must contain 97 % and the bottoms 2 %. Find the distillate flow. D kmol/h D = 250 × (0.35 − 0.02)/(0.97 − 0.02) = 86.8 kmol/h Recovery of the light component in the distillate: 86.8 × 0.97 / 87.5 = 96.3 %.

A saturated-liquid feed with z F = 0.50 is split to x D = 0.98. The relative volatility is constant at 2.2. Find R min . R min – R_min = [0.98/0.50 − 2.2 × 0.02/0.50] / (2.2 − 1) = (1.960 − 0.088)/1.2 = 1.56 Check it in Figure 1 with constant α = 2.2: the tile shows the same value.

For the same mixture, x D = 0.98 and x B = 0.03. Find the minimum number of theoretical stages, including the reboiler. N min stages N_min = ln[(0.98/0.02)(0.97/0.03)] / ln 2.2 = ln(1,584.3)/0.7885 = 9.34

A liquid feed enters at 55 °C. Its bubble point is 95 °C, its heat capacity 160 kJ/(kmol·K) and its latent heat 32,000 kJ/kmol. Find q. q – q = 1 + 160 × (95 − 55)/32,000 = 1.20; q-line slope = q/(q − 1) = 6 The extra 0.2 F of liquid below the feed is vapour condensed by the cold feed: the stripping section carries more liquid and the rectifying section less vapour.

entries.h: Problem 5. Stages at a real reflux ratio
entries.x: With R min = 1.56 and N min = 9.34 from Problems 2 and 3, estimate the theoretical stages (including the reboiler) at R = 2.0 with Molokanov’s equation. N stages X = (2.0 − 1.56)/3.0 = 0.1467 Y = 1 − exp{[(1 + 54.4 × 0.1467)/(11 + 117.2 × 0.1467)] × [(0.1467 − 1)/√0.1467]} = 0.508 N = (9.34 + 0.508)/(1 − 0.508) = 20.0

A column needs 20 theoretical trays (excluding the reboiler). The keys have α = 1.9 and the liquid viscosity at the average temperature is 0.35 mPa·s. How many actual trays does O’Connell’s correlation give? Round up. Trays trays E_o = 0.492 × (1.9 × 0.35)^−0.245 = 0.544; 20 / 0.544 = 36.8 → 37 trays

entries.h: Problem 7. Flooding velocity at high pressure
entries.x: From Fair’s chart C SB = 0.085 m/s. The liquid has ρ L = 650 kg/m³ and σ = 15 mN/m; the vapour has ρ V = 12 kg/m³. Find the flooding velocity on the net area (non-foaming, hole area 10 %). u n,f m/s u_nf = 0.085 × (15/20)^0.2 × √((650 − 12)/12) = 0.085 × 0.944 × 7.29 = 0.585 m/s Dense vapour cuts the flooding velocity sharply; that is why high-pressure columns are wide for their mass flow.

entries.h: Problem 8. Diameter from the vapour volume
entries.x: A column carries 2.4 m³/s of vapour at a design velocity of 1.2 m/s on the net area. Downcomers take 12 % of the area. Find the diameter. D m A_n = 2.4/1.2 = 2.00 m²; A_c = 2.00/0.88 = 2.27 m² D = √(4 × 2.27/π) = 1.70 m
A tray passes 12 kg/s of liquid with ρ L = 780 kg/m³ over a 1.2 m weir. Find the weir crest. h ow mm h_ow = 750 × [12/(780 × 1.2)]^(2/3) = 750 × 0.0548 = 41.1 mm of liquid

Vapour passes the holes at 15 m/s with ρ V = 3 kg/m³ over liquid of 800 kg/m³. The orifice coefficient is 0.84. Find the dry-tray head. h d mm h_d = 51 × (15/0.84)² × 3/800 = 51 × 318.9 × 0.00375 = 61.0 mm of liquid The hole F-factor is 15 × √3 = 26 Pa 0.5 , comfortably above the weeping limits of equation (38).

A tray has h w = 50 mm, h ow = 12 mm, a total tray drop h t = 110 mm and a head loss under the downcomer h dc = 8 mm, all as liquid. The tray spacing is 600 mm. Find the clear-liquid backup h b . h b mm h_b = (50 + 12) + 110 + 8 = 180 mm; limit ½(600 + 50) = 325 mm → 55 % of the limit

An organic separation needs 18 theoretical stages. Estimate the packed height with a Y-type structured packing of 250 m²/m³ using Kister’s rule. Z m HETP = 100/250 + 0.1 = 0.50 m; Z = 18 × 0.50 = 9.0 m For an aqueous system the rule doubles the HETP to 1.0 m and the height to 18 m. Split long sections into beds with redistributors.

entries.h: Problem 13. Pressure drop at flood in a packed bed
entries.x: A packing has a packing factor of 18 ft⁻¹. Find the pressure drop at flood from Kister and Gill’s equation, in mbar per metre. ΔP flood mbar/m ΔP = 0.12 × 18^0.7 = 0.908 in. H₂O/ft × 83.3 = 75.6 mm H₂O/m × 0.0981 = 7.4 mbar/m The equation is in US units; convert only at the end.

entries.h: Problem 14. Relief load for loss of cooling
entries.x: A column’s reboiler delivers 2.5 MW. The overhead vapour’s latent heat at relieving conditions is 300 kJ/kg. Estimate the relief load by the unbalanced-heat method, with no credits. W kg/h W = 2,500 kW / 300 kJ/kg = 8.33 kg/s = 30,000 kg/h If the heating medium is steam at a fixed temperature, the reboiler duty falls as the column temperature rises at relieving pressure; that “pinch” is a legitimate credit if it is calculated.

A column has a design pressure of 1.2 MPa gauge and an inside diameter of 2,400 mm; SA-516-70 at 138 MPa, full radiography (E = 1.0), corrosion allowance 3 mm. Find the required thickness including the allowance. t mm R = 1,200 + 3 = 1,203 mm t = 1.2 × 1,203 / (138 × 1.0 − 0.6 × 1.2) + 3 = 10.5 + 3 = 13.5 mm → order 14 mm or more

entries.h: Problem 16. Cooling water for the condenser
entries.x: A condenser removes 4.2 MW. Cooling water may rise 10 K (c p = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)). Find the water flow. m kg/s m = 4,200 / (4.18 × 10) = 100.5 kg/s ≈ 362 m³/h

entries.h: Problem 17. Minimum boil-up in a stripper
entries.x: A reboiled stripper with no reflux takes a saturated-liquid feed of z F = 0.20 on its top tray; α = 4. The bottoms must reach x B = 0.005. Find the minimum boil-up as V̄/F. (V̄/F) min – y*(0.20) = 0.8/1.6 = 0.500 (L̄/V̄)_max = (0.500 − 0.005)/(0.20 − 0.005) = 2.538 → (V̄/F)_min = 1/2.538 = 0.394 Check it in Figure 1: stripper, constant α = 4, z F = 0.20, x B = 0.005.

entries.h: Problem 18. The hydrochloric acid azeotrope in mole fraction
entries.x: Constant-boiling hydrochloric acid at 101.3 kPa is 20.2 wt % HCl. Convert to mole fraction HCl (M = 36.46 and 18.02). x HCl – x = (20.2/36.46) / (20.2/36.46 + 79.8/18.02) = 0.554/(0.554 + 4.430) = 0.111 A maximum-boiling azeotrope: distilling dilute acid sends water overhead and leaves the bottoms at this composition.

entries.h: Problem 19. Which stream should hold the drum level?
entries.x: A propylene–propane splitter runs at a reflux ratio L/D of 15 with the LV scheme of Figure 8: LIC-111 sets the distillate flow. At turndown the drum level swings and FV-110 works between 5 and 15 % open. What would you change on the P&ID, and what does the change do to the composition control? The distillate is one sixteenth of the liquid leaving the drum, so a small error in the reflux flow is a large error in level, and the distillate valve works near its closed end, where it controls badly. Hold the level with the largest stream: move LIC-111 onto the reflux set point (the DV scheme). The distillate then becomes a composition handle, set by a rectifying-section temperature ( TIC-120 ) or, on a splitter where the tray temperatures barely change, by the analyser AI-108 through a slow cascade. The price is that reflux now moves only through the level loop, so LIC-111 must be tuned tight, and its tuning now affects how the column responds to composition moves. Select DV in Figure 8 to see the new cascades.

entries.h: Problem 20. Spot the problem on the P&ID
entries.x: A draft P&ID shows the column’s high-high pressure trip taking its signal from PT-101 , the pressure controller’s transmitter, and closing FV-106 , the steam control valve, through a solenoid. The PSV has been deleted “because the trip now protects the column”. List what is wrong and how you would fix it. Three problems. The trip shares its transmitter with PIC-101 : if PT-101 reads low, the controller lets the pressure rise and the trip never sees it. It shares its valve with the control loop: if FV-106 sticks open, nothing stops the steam. Neither counts as an independent layer. The fix is the layout in Figure 8: a separate PT-116 into the SIS, logic in interlock I-100 , and a separate XV-117 in series with FV-106 , also closing the feed. Set the trip between the PIC high alarm and the relief set pressure. Keep the PSV: it is still required by the pressure-vessel code and is the last layer, sized for the governing API 521 case. 19

entries.h: What goes on the column data sheet
entries.x: The process data sheet is where a column design becomes an enquiry to the internals vendor and the vessel fabricator. Give every case that matters, not only the normal one. Service and cases. Tag, service, and every case: normal, maximum, minimum (turndown), start-up and any alternate feeds. Separation. Feed composition and condition; product specifications as purities and recoveries; the key components. Stage requirements. Theoretical stages per section, feed and draw locations, assumed efficiency or HETP and its basis. Loads per section. Top and bottom of each section: vapour and liquid mass flows, densities, viscosities, surface tension, molar masses, temperatures and pressures. System behaviour. Foaming tendency and system factor, fouling, solids, polymerisation, corrosion, two liquid phases. Internals. Tray type and number of passes or packing type; tray spacing; minimum turndown; allowable pressure drop; feed and draw devices; distributors. Conditions. Operating and design pressure and temperature, minimum design metal temperature, vacuum design (full or partial). Exchangers. Condenser and reboiler duties for each case, type (thermosiphon, kettle, fired), heating and cooling media. Nozzles and levels. Nozzle schedule; sump hold-up; normal, alarm and trip levels; reboiler return elevation; independent level connections. Control and instrumentation. Pressure-control method, which streams hold the levels, the temperature-control tray and spare thermowells, analyser sample points, and trip set points. Relief. Set pressure and the governing case, with loss of cooling, loss of reflux, power failure and fire noted. Materials. Shell, internals and packing materials; corrosion allowance; cladding; sour service. Codes. ASME VIII (or the contract code), CSA B51 registration if installed in Canada, wind and seismic basis, owner standards. 20
