A centrifugal pump that can be throttled to zero flow by its own control valve, by a closed downstream isolation valve or by a tripped reactor needs a way to keep its flow above the vendor's minimum. A recycle line from the discharge back to the suction source is the standard answer, and it is both a safety and a process control feature: it prevents the deadhead heating of section 12 and lets the forward flow be turned down to zero without starting and stopping the pump. Where it goes matters as much as having one: Measure total pump flow. Put the minimum-flow flowmeter upstream of the recycle tee, so it sees forward plus recycled flow, and control that total, not the forward flow. Return to the suction vessel, not the suction line. The tank inventory absorbs the heat; a short loop back to the pump suction does not. 44 Example 9 shows the difference: about 0.7 K per hour in the tank, against about 11 K per minute in a 20 L suction loop. Return below the liquid surface through a dip pipe or a low nozzle. It avoids flashing at the inlet and, for a static-accumulating liquid such as toluene, avoids splash filling. If the return must go into the vapour space, take the pressure drop in a multi-stage orifice. 45 Let a restriction orifice take most of the pressure drop and leave the control valve a modest share, so the valve controls well and erodes slowly. Make the minimum-flow valve fail open. Losing air then costs energy, not a pump. Size for the worst case: the highest discharge pressure (lowest flow, highest suction pressure) and the lowest back pressure. One protection per pump. For pumps that run in parallel, each needs its own flow measurement and recycle; a common one on the header cannot see whether one pump is being pushed back towards shutoff. Four methods are in common use. They all keep the total pump flow above the minimum; they differ in how much energy they waste and how much instrumentation they need. 41 How low is the minimum? Typical published minimum continuous flows are 25–40 % of BEP for low specific speed end-suction pumps and higher for high-energy and high specific speed designs. 51 Always take the number from the vendor's curve for the pump you buy. Table 5. Ways to keep a centrifugal pump above its minimum flow. Method How it works Advantages Drawbacks Continuous orifice bypass A restriction orifice returns a fixed flow to the suction vessel all the time Simple, cheap, no instruments, nothing to fail Wastes power continuously; the bypass flow must be added to the rated flow, so the pump and motor get bigger Modulating control valve (Figure 8) A flow transmitter on total pump flow drives a control valve and orifice in the recycle line Recycles only what is needed; adjustable; flow is indicated in the control room Flowmeter, controller and valve to maintain; needs a backup trip if the valve fails shut On/off valve and flow switch A low-flow switch opens a valve in the recycle line; an orifice limits the flow Cheaper than a modulating loop Cycles between open and shut near the setpoint; jumps in flow upset the process Automatic recirculation valve A self-acting valve at the pump discharge: its flow-sensing check disc opens a bypass as main flow falls, replacing the discharge check valve 42 43 No external power or instruments; combines check, bypass, control and pressure letdown in one body 41 Custom-sized to one pump; a single supplier part to stock; flow is not indicated unless a meter is added

entries.h: Upstream and downstream: what sets the pump's operating point
entries.x: The pump in Figure 8 does not control anything by itself. Upstream, PCV-104 and the tank level fix its suction pressure; downstream, PIC-201 fixes the reactor pressure and FIC-108 chooses the flow. Together they place the operating point on the pump curve, exactly as in Figure 1. Change any one of them and the operating point moves, so the HAZOP has to ask what each one does when it fails. When the suction vessel is a process drum rather than a storage tank, the usual scheme is a cascade: the drum level controller sets the setpoint of the pump discharge flow controller, so flow disturbances are corrected quickly and level is corrected slowly. Boiler drums use the same idea, with a level controller cascaded into a feedwater flow controller. 49 The minimum-flow loop then sits underneath, unchanged.

Pressure-triggered auto-start is the most common arrangement because a pressure transmitter is cheaper and more robust than a flowmeter. The setpoint is a compromise: low enough that a normal dip, such as the running pump moving to run-out, does not start the spare, and high enough that a real trip always does. 46 Two details are easy to miss. The spare must be lined up, full and, in hot service, warm, or the auto-start starts a dry or blocked-in pump. And the trips that stop a pump for a process reason, such as low-low level or a closed suction valve, must block the auto-start, or the spare starts into the same problem a few seconds later.

A large inventory of flammable or toxic liquid connected to a pump is a hazard if a seal or a flange fails, because nobody can safely walk into a pump fire to shut a manual valve. A remotely operated shutoff valve on the vessel outlet lets the operator isolate the inventory from the control room; the UK HSE's HSG244 sets out how to decide whether one is needed and how to specify it. 47 Refiners often place them in pump suction lines, for example for liquids above their autoignition temperature or with high H₂S, and rate them for the pump shutoff pressure because a leaking check valve can expose them to discharge pressure. 48 Closing the valve on a running pump starves it, so its closed position switch trips the pump.

entries.h: A P&ID review checklist for a pump
entries.x: Suction: vessel elevation and low-low level support the NPSH calculation at maximum flow; no high points; straight run and long-radius elbow at the nozzle; temporary strainer with a way to see its pressure drop. Each pump: suction and discharge isolation, a check valve upstream of the discharge isolation valve, a discharge pressure gauge, vent and drain to a closed system for hazardous liquids. Minimum flow: flowmeter on total pump flow, recycle to the suction vessel, valve fail-safe position, orifice, low-flow trip as backup. Seal: the API 682 arrangement and piping plan for the hazard, with its alarms routed to the control room. Pressure: piping and equipment up to the first relief device rated for maximum suction pressure plus shutoff head with the largest impeller and highest density; thermal relief where liquid can be blocked in. Spare: auto-start logic, the trips that block it, and how the operator knows which pump is lined up. Downstream: control valve fail position chosen for the process, check valve against reverse flow from a pressurized receiver, shutdown valve for the receiver's trips. Minimum-flow return and level control. Because the recycle goes back to the same tank, it does not change the tank's level balance; only the forward flow does. If the recycle went to a different vessel, the level controllers of both vessels would see it. 14

Each example is a situation I have met, with the numbers simplified. Examples 3 to 6 and 8 use the illustrative pump of Figure 1: H = 60 − 0.001Q² (Q in m³/h, H in m) at 3,550 rpm with a 250 mm impeller, BEP at 100 m³/h, 50 m and 78 %.

entries.h: Example 1. NPSH for a reflux pump on a drum at its bubble point
entries.x: Given Reflux drum at 1,200 kPa(a), liquid at its bubble point. Low-low liquid level 4.5 m above the pump centreline. Suction losses 0.6 m at rated flow. Vendor NPSH3: 2.8 m at rated flow, 3.5 m at 120 % of rated. Hydrocarbon service. Find Whether NPSHa meets ANSI/HI 9.6.1 at rated flow and at 120 % flow. The liquid is saturated, so p surface = p v and the pressure term in equation (7) is zero. At rated flow: NPSHa = 0 + 4.5 − 0.6 = 3.9 m Required, hydrocarbon process (ratio 1.1 or 1.0 m, whichever is greater): max(1.1 × 2.8, 2.8 + 1.0) = max(3.08, 3.80) = 3.80 m ≤ 3.9 m → acceptable, just At 120 % flow, losses scale with Q²: h f = 0.6 × 1.2² = 0.86 m; NPSHa = 4.5 − 0.86 = 3.64 m Required at 120 %: max(1.1 × 3.5, 3.5 + 1.0) = 4.50 m > 3.64 m → not acceptable Liquid height needed: z ≥ 4.50 + 0.86 = 5.36 m Raise the drum by about 0.9 m, choose a pump with lower NPSH3 at high flow, or limit the maximum flow. NPSHa falls and NPSH3 rises as flow increases. Check at the highest flow the pump will see, with the lowest level, and remember that pressurizing a bubble-point drum adds nothing.

entries.h: Example 2. Sizing a toluene transfer pump
entries.x: Liquid Toluene at 25 °C: ρ = 862 kg/m³, μ = 0.56 mPa·s, p v = 3.79 kPa(a). Route Atmospheric tank (minimum level 1.5 m above pump centreline) to a reactor at 300 kPa(g), inlet nozzle 14.0 m above pump centreline. Flows Normal 30 m³/h; rated 33 m³/h (110 % of normal). Suction 4 in Sch 40 (102.3 mm bore), 6 m, tank entrance, one gate valve, two long-radius elbows. Discharge 3 in Sch 40 (77.9 mm bore), 45 m, swing check, two gate valves, six long-radius elbows, exit into reactor. Control valve allowance 70 kPa and flowmeter 20 kPa at rated flow. Roughness 0.046 mm. Find Rated head, differential pressure, shaft power, motor size and NPSHa. Velocities at 33 m³/h: v s = 1.12 m/s, v d = 1.92 m/s Reynolds numbers and friction factors (Swamee–Jain): Re s = 1.76×10⁵, f s = 0.0189; Re d = 2.31×10⁵, f d = 0.0192 Fitting coefficients: ΣK s = 0.5 + 8(0.017) + 2×14(0.017) = 1.11 ΣK d = 100(0.018) + 2×8(0.018) + 6×14(0.018) + 1.0 = 4.60 Line losses: h f,s = (1.11 + 1.11) × 0.064 = 0.14 m; h f,d = (11.07 + 4.60) × 0.188 = 2.95 m Static head: 300,000 / (862 × 9.81) + (14.0 − 1.5) = 35.48 + 12.50 = 47.98 m Control valve and flowmeter: 70,000 / (862 × 9.81) = 8.28 m; 20,000 / (862 × 9.81) = 2.37 m Rated total head: H = 47.98 + 0.14 + 2.95 + 8.28 + 2.37 = 61.7 m; Δp = 862 × 9.81 × 61.7 = 5.22 bar Power with 62 % efficiency read from a vendor curve: P h = 862 × 9.81 × (33/3600) × 61.7 = 4.78 kW; P shaft = 4.78 / 0.62 = 7.72 kW Motor: 7.5 kW is too small; check the end-of-curve power on the vendor curve and select the next standard size, 11 kW. NPSHa: (101,325 − 3,790) / (862 × 9.81) + 1.5 − 0.14 = 11.53 + 1.36 = 12.9 m Plenty of margin. 78 % of this head is static. The control valve is the largest dynamic term, so a VFD would save little; the right pump is an ASME B73.1 end-suction pump rated 33 m³/h at 62 m, with a seal arrangement chosen for a flammable liquid.

Given Illustrative pump; system H = 30 + 0.002Q². At full speed the pump delivers 100 m³/h. The process now needs 80 m³/h for most of the year. Find Shaft power by throttling and by speed reduction, and what 80 % speed actually delivers. System head at 80 m³/h: H sys = 30 + 0.002 × 80² = 42.8 m Throttling at full speed: H pump = 60 − 0.001 × 80² = 53.6 m; x = 0.80; η = 0.78(2x − x²) = 74.9 % P = 1000 × 9.81 × (80/3600) × 53.6 / 0.749 = 15.6 kW The valve burns 53.6 − 42.8 = 10.8 m. Speed reduction: find s = N/N 0 so the pump makes 42.8 m at 80 m³/h: 60s² − 0.001 × 80² = 42.8 → s = 0.906 → 3,215 rpm x = 80/(100 × 0.906) = 0.883; η = 76.9 %; P = 9.81 × (80/3600) × 42.8 / 0.769 = 12.1 kW Saving: 15.6 − 12.1 = 3.5 kW ≈ 28 MWh/yr at 8,000 h ≈ $2,800/yr at $0.10/kWh (illustrative), before drive losses At 80 % speed the pump's shutoff head is 60 × 0.8² = 38.4 m, barely above the 30 m static head: Q = √[(38.4 − 30)/(0.001 + 0.002)] = 52.9 m³/h, not 80 Speed reduction saves energy here, but far less than the cube law suggests, and the speed needed is set by the system curve, not by the affinity laws alone.

Given The illustrative pump was bought with a 250 mm impeller, but the line only needs 100 m³/h at 42 m. Operators throttle the discharge valve to get there. Find The trimmed diameter and the power saved. Draw the trim parabola through the new duty: H = (42/100²) Q² = 0.0042 Q² Intersect it with the full-diameter curve: 60 − 0.001Q² = 0.0042Q² → Q 1 = 107.4 m³/h, H 1 = 48.5 m Diameter law: D 2 = 250 × 100/107.4 = 232.7 mm (check: 250 × √(42/48.5) = 232.7 mm) Order 235 mm, test, then trim further if needed. Power: throttled full impeller at 100 m³/h absorbs 17.5 kW at 50 m. Trimmed, at 42 m and about 77.6 %: P = 9.81 × (100/3600) × 42 / 0.776 = 14.8 kW → saving 2.7 kW Do not scale diameter by the head ratio at constant flow; scale along the parabola through the origin. Before trimming, recheck NPSH3, minimum flow and the 5 % head-growth margin you will give up.

entries.h: Example 5. Adding a second pump in parallel
entries.x: Given One illustrative pump on the system H = 30 + 0.002Q² delivers 100 m³/h. Production wants more and an identical spare is available. Find Flow with both running and where each pump operates. Combined curve for two identical pumps: at head H each delivers q, so Q = 2q: H = 60 − 0.001 (Q/2)² = 60 − 0.00025 Q² Intersect with the system: 60 − 0.00025Q² = 30 + 0.002Q² → Q = 115.5 m³/h, H = 56.7 m Each pump: q = 57.7 m³/h = 58 % of BEP; η = 0.78(2 × 0.577 − 0.577²) = 64 % A 15 % gain, with both pumps outside their preferred region. The fixes are a pump selected for the two-pump duty, impellers matched to the higher head, or a different arrangement. See Figure 5.

entries.h: Example 6. How fast a blocked-in pump heats up
entries.x: Given The illustrative pump is started with both valves closed. Its power curve gives 10.5 kW at zero flow. The casing holds about 15 L of water at 25 °C and about 60 kg of wetted steel (c p 0.5 kJ/kg·K). Find The heating rate and time to 100 °C, ignoring heat loss to air; then the temperature rise at 30 % of BEP flow. Liquid only: dT/dt = 10,480 / (15 × 4,180) = 0.167 K/s ≈ 10 K/min → 25 to 100 °C in about 7.5 min With the steel heated too: dT/dt = 10,480 / (15 × 4,180 + 60 × 500) = 0.113 K/s ≈ 6.8 K/min → about 11 min At 30 % of BEP flow (30 m³/h, H = 59.1 m, η = 39.8 %), the liquid passes through and the rise is small: 14 ΔT = 9.81 × 59.1 × (1/0.398 − 1) / 4,180 = 0.21 K With flow, the temperature rise is a fraction of a kelvin; without it, a casing can reach boiling in minutes. For a hydrocarbon near its bubble point, even 1–2 K of heating at low flow can use up the NPSH margin.

entries.h: Example 7. Acceleration head for a triplex plunger pump
entries.x: Given Triplex plunger pump injecting lean amine at 40 L/min, crank speed 120 rpm. Suction line 6 m of 1 in Sch 40 (26.6 mm bore). K = 1.5. Find Acceleration head, and the effect of a simplex pump or a 2 in suction line. Velocity: V = (40/60,000) / (π × 0.0266²/4) = 1.20 m/s Triplex, C = 0.066: h a = 6 × 1.20 × 120 × 0.066 / (1.5 × 9.81) = 3.9 m Simplex, C = 0.400: h a = 23.4 m Triplex on 2 in Sch 40 (52.5 mm bore, V = 0.31 m/s): h a = 1.0 m Acceleration head is subtracted from NPSHa and can exceed every other suction term. More plungers and larger, shorter suction lines are the cheapest cures. See Figure 7.

entries.h: Example 8. The same pump on a viscous oil
entries.x: Given Illustrative pump, water BEP 100 m³/h at 50 m and 78 %, 3,550 rpm. Oil at 200 cSt, relative density 0.90. Find Viscous BEP and shaft power using ANSI/HI 9.6.7. Parameter B, equation (13): B = 16.5 × 14.14 × 1.277 / (5.623 × 7.719) = 6.86 Correction factors, equation (14): C Q = exp[−0.165 × (0.8367) 3.15 ] = 0.910; C H at BEP = 0.910; C η = 6.86 −0.0547 × 6.86 0.69 = 0.672 Viscous BEP: Q = 91.0 m³/h; H = 45.5 m; η = 0.672 × 78 % = 52.4 % Power: P = 900 × 9.81 × (91.0/3600) × 45.5 / 0.524 = 19.4 kW The water curve corrected only for density would suggest 15.7 kW. Viscosity hits efficiency and power much harder than head. Size the motor for the coldest, thickest case, and compare against a rotary PD pump when B is high.

entries.h: Example 9. Sizing the minimum-flow recycle for the toluene pump
entries.x: Given The pump of Example 2 and Figure 8. The (illustrative) vendor curve is H = 72 − 0.00918Q², rated 33 m³/h at 62 m, with a minimum continuous stable flow of 10 m³/h at 71.1 m and 30 % efficiency. Toluene ρ = 862 kg/m³, c p = 1.70 kJ/kg·K. Tank at atmospheric pressure, minimum level 1.5 m above the pump centreline. The recycle is 1½ in Sch 40 (40.9 mm bore), 25 m equivalent length, entering the tank through a nozzle 0.3 m above the pump centreline. Find The pressure drop available to FV-107 and RO-107, the orifice bore, and where the heat goes. Suction and discharge pressure at 10 m³/h (suction losses negligible): p_s = 101.3 + 862 × 9.81 × 1.5/1000 = 114.0 kPa(a) p_d = 114.0 + 862 × 9.81 × 71.1/1000 = 715.1 kPa(a) Back pressure at the return nozzle, with 1.2 m of liquid above it at minimum level: 101.3 + 862 × 9.81 × 1.2/1000 = 111.5 kPa(a); nozzle elevation 0.3 m = 2.5 kPa Recycle line friction at 10 m³/h: v = 2.12 m/s; Re = 1.33×10⁵; f = 0.0222 h_f = 0.0222 × 25/0.0409 × 2.12²/(2 × 9.81) = 3.1 m = 26.2 kPa Pressure drop left for the valve and orifice: 715.1 − 111.5 − 2.5 − 26.2 = 574.9 kPa Give FV-107 about 100 kPa at full recycle for control, and the orifice the rest, 475 kPa. Orifice bore with C d = 0.61: A = (10/3600) / [0.61 × √(2 × 475,000/862)] = 1.37×10⁻⁴ m² → d = 13.2 mm, β = 0.32 The orifice drops 475 kPa into a downstream pressure of only about 140 kPa(a). A single plate with that ratio is likely to cavitate, so specify a multi-stage orifice (three plates of about 160 kPa each) and confirm with the orifice supplier. 45 Heat. All the power at minimum flow ends up in the liquid: P = 862 × 9.81 × (10/3600) × 71.1 / 0.30 = 5.57 kW ΔT per pass = 5,570 / (2.394 kg/s × 1,700) = 1.4 K Returned to T-101 with 20 m³ (17.2 t) at minimum level: 5,570 × 3,600 / (17,240 × 1,700) = 0.7 K per hour Returned to a 20 L loop at the pump suction instead, the same liquid passes every 7 s: 1.4 K per pass ≈ 11 K per minute, with nothing to remove it The recycle is cheap insurance: a 1½ in line, a small valve and a stack of orifice plates keep the pump alive at zero forward flow. Its destination matters as much as its size. Into the tank, the heat is negligible; into the suction line, it boils the pump within minutes. 15
Work each one before opening the solution. Answers are accepted within 2 %. Where a problem uses "the illustrative pump", it means H = 60 − 0.001Q², η = 0.78(2x − x²) with x = Q/100, at 3,550 rpm.

A pump raises 50 % ethylene glycol (relative density 1.07) by 8.5 bar. What head does it develop? What differential pressure would the same pump give on water (relative density 0.998)? Head m H = 850,000 / (1,070 × 9.81) = 81.0 m. On water: Δp = 998 × 9.81 × 81.0 = 7.93 bar. Same head, lower pressure, lower power.

entries.h: Problem 2. Suction lift with warm water
entries.x: A pump lifts water at 60 °C (ρ = 983 kg/m³, p v = 19.95 kPa) from an open sump at sea level. The water surface is 3.0 m below the impeller eye and suction losses are 0.8 m. Find NPSHa. NPSHa m (101,325 − 19,950)/(983 × 9.81) − 3.0 − 0.8 = 8.44 − 3.80 = 4.64 m At 60 °C, vapour pressure has taken almost 2 m off the atmospheric term. Hot water and suction lift do not mix well.

entries.h: Problem 3. Butane sphere at low level
entries.x: A butane transfer pump takes suction from a sphere at the vapour pressure of its contents. At normal level the liquid is 6.0 m above the pump centreline; suction losses are 1.2 m. What is NPSHa if operators draw the level down to 2.0 m above the centreline? NPSHa m Normal: 6.0 − 1.2 = 4.8 m. Low level: 2.0 − 1.2 = 0.8 m. The pressure term is zero for a saturated liquid. The safeguard is a low-level trip set from the NPSH calculation, not from the tank's mechanical minimum.

entries.h: Problem 4. A 60 Hz pump on a 50 Hz supply
entries.x: A pump rated 200 m³/h at 30 m and 22 kW at 1,780 rpm is moved to a site where the motor will run at 1,480 rpm. Estimate the new flow, head and shaft power at the equivalent point. Enter the power. Shaft power kW r = 1480/1780 = 0.831; Q = 166 m³/h; H = 30 × 0.691 = 20.7 m; P = 22 × 0.575 = 12.6 kW The pump loses 31 % of its head. Whether it still meets the duty depends on the system curve, which is the real question to ask.

Two illustrative pumps run in series on the system H = 30 + 0.002Q². Find the flow. Is that acceptable for the pumps? Flow m³/h 2(60 − 0.001Q²) = 30 + 0.002Q² → 90 = 0.004Q² → Q = 150 m³/h, H = 75 m Each pump runs at 150 % of BEP, beyond the end of its curve at 130 %: cavitation and motor overload. Series pumps must be selected for the series duty.

The illustrative pump is rated at its BEP (17.5 kW on water) but its curve runs to 130 m³/h. What shaft power does it absorb at the end of the curve, and which IEC motor size (15, 18.5, 22, 30 kW) is non-overloading? Power at end of curve kW H = 60 − 0.001 × 130² = 43.1 m; x = 1.3; η = 0.78(2.6 − 1.69) = 0.710 P = 9.81 × (130/3600) × 43.1 / 0.710 = 21.5 kW → 22 kW motor An 18.5 kW motor covers the rated point only.

entries.h: Problem 7. Temperature rise at minimum flow
entries.x: A hydrocarbon pump (c p = 2.2 kJ/kg·K) develops 150 m at its minimum flow, where its efficiency is 30 %. Find the temperature rise through the pump. Temperature rise K ΔT = 9.81 × 150 × (1/0.30 − 1) / 2,200 = 1.56 K Check what 1.6 K does to the vapour pressure of the recycled liquid if the bypass returns to the suction line instead of the vessel.

A single-acting duplex diaphragm pump (C = 0.200) runs at 90 strokes per minute and draws water at 20 °C (ρ = 998 kg/m³, p v = 2.34 kPa) from an atmospheric tank with its surface 2.0 m above the pump. The suction line is 10 m long with a mean velocity of 0.8 m/s and 0.5 m of losses. Use K = 1.4. Find the NPSHa left after acceleration head. Net NPSHa m Static NPSHa = (101,325 − 2,339)/(998 × 9.81) + 2.0 − 0.5 = 11.61 m h_a = 10 × 0.8 × 90 × 0.200 / (1.4 × 9.81) = 10.48 m; net = 1.1 m Almost all the margin is gone. A suction stabilizer, a shorter or larger line, or a triplex would fix it.

entries.h: Problem 9. A low specific speed duty
entries.x: A duty needs 25 m³/h at 120 m. Calculate n q for a single-stage pump at 3,550 rpm, and for a two-stage pump. Enter the single-stage value. n q – n_q = 3550 × √(25/3600) / 120^0.75 = 3550 × 0.0833 / 36.3 = 8.2 (about 420 in US units) Two stages of 60 m: n_q = 13.7 At about 420 in US units a single-stage radial pump is in the region where PD pumps are often considered, and its efficiency will be poor. A two-stage pump, a high-speed OH6, or a PD pump is worth pricing.

entries.h: Problem 10. Is this vendor's selection acceptable?
entries.x: Normal flow is 70 m³/h and rated flow 80 m³/h. The vendor offers an API 610 pump whose BEP with the furnished impeller is 105 m³/h. Rated flow as a percentage of BEP? Rated / BEP % 80/105 = 76 % (outside 80–110 %); normal 70/105 = 67 % (outside the 70–120 % POR) Reject it, or ask for a smaller pump or impeller. The pump would spend its life left of the preferred region.

A chemical process pump has NPSH3 = 3.2 m and the system gives NPSHa = 3.6 m. Using the conservative end of the HI chemical range (ratio 1.2 or 1.0 m), what minimum NPSHa is recommended? Minimum NPSHa m max(1.2 × 3.2, 3.2 + 1.0) = max(3.84, 4.20) = 4.2 m. Present: ratio 1.13, margin 0.4 m. It fails even the low end of the range (max(1.1 × 3.2, 3.2 + 0.6) = 3.8 m).

A triplex pump has 40 mm plungers, a 75 mm stroke and runs at 180 rpm with 95 % volumetric efficiency. Find the delivered flow. Flow m³/h Q = 3 × (π × 0.040²/4) × 0.075 × 180 × 60 × 0.95 = 2.90 m³/h The relief valve downstream must pass all 2.90 m³/h at relieving pressure.

entries.h: Problem 13. Where does the relief valve go?
entries.x: A gear pump discharges through a filter, a block valve and a flowmeter to a blending header. Where should the relief valve be, what capacity should it have, and where should it discharge? Between the pump and the first device that can block flow, here upstream of the filter (which can plug) and the block valve. Size it for the full pump capacity at relieving conditions, with the set pressure and accumulation below the design pressure of the pump and piping. Route it to the suction vessel, not the pump suction line. The pump's internal relief valve, if fitted, protects the pump only.

An operator controls a centrifugal pump by pinching the suction valve "because it is closer". Explain what happens and what to do instead. Throttling the suction adds a loss term to equation (7), so NPSHa falls while NPSH3 stays the same. The pump cavitates, the head drops erratically, and the seal and bearings suffer. It can also flash the liquid in the suction line. Control on the discharge, with a variable-speed drive, or with a bypass to the suction vessel, and keep suction valves fully open.

entries.h: Problem 15. A restriction orifice for a water pump
entries.x: A water pump (ρ = 998 kg/m³) needs a minimum-flow recycle of 12 m³/h. After the control valve and line losses, 3.0 bar is left for a single-plate restriction orifice with C d = 0.61. What bore does the orifice need? Bore mm A = (12/3600) / [0.61 × √(2 × 300,000/998)] = 0.003333 / 14.96 = 2.23×10⁻⁴ m² d = √(4A/π) = 16.8 mm Check the downstream pressure before accepting a single plate: if the ratio across it is high, use several plates in series.

entries.h: Problem 16. The auto-start that made it worse
entries.x: In a HAZOP of Figure 8, someone proposes deleting the "block standby auto-start" column from Table 4 to simplify the logic. What happens on a low-low tank level if you agree? LSLL-102 trips P-101A, discharge pressure falls, and PALL-106 starts P-101B through I-2. The spare now runs on a tank that is still at low-low level, so it loses NPSH margin, cavitates and may run dry, which can fail its seal and release toluene. Any trip that stops a pump for a process reason (low-low level, closed suction valve, low-low flow) must also block the auto-start; only faults of the pump itself (motor, seal, vibration) should start the spare. 16

The process engineer owns the process side of the datasheet. A pump is only as good as the data it was selected for, so I fill in every line below before a vendor sees it. Liquid: name and composition, including trace and dissolved components Temperatures: normal, minimum and maximum pumping temperature Properties at each temperature: density, viscosity, vapour pressure, specific heat Solids: concentration, size, hardness; entrained gas Hazards: flammability, toxicity, autoignition temperature, corrosion, polymerization or crystallization Flows: minimum, normal and rated, with the basis for each margin Suction pressure: minimum, normal and maximum, with vessel levels Discharge pressure: at rated flow, and the maximum the system can impose NPSHa: value, datum (impeller eye or grade) and the flow it was calculated at Operation: continuous or intermittent, parallel or series, spare philosophy, auto-start Standards and seals: API 610 or ASME B73, API 682 arrangement and plan, or sealless Materials: casing and impeller class for the corrosion and erosion duty Driver: motor or turbine, voltage, VFD, area classification Instruments: minimum-flow protection and its method (section 13), trips and alarms, vibration and temperature monitoring Site: elevation, ambient range, winterization (heat tracing, insulation) Testing: performance and NPSH tests, acceptance grade, witness points 17

Lessons / Process economics / Techno-economic analysis Techno-economic analysis, from an equipment list to a selling price How a process engineer turns a flowsheet into a number a decision can rest on, with one hydrogen plant worked through from purchased equipment to the minimum selling price. Alireza Lotfollahzade , EIT Updated 15 November 2026 About 30 minutes to read Take an illustrative hydrogen plant: $400 million of total overnight capital, 30,000 t of hydrogen a year, $18 million a year of fixed operating cost and $65 million a year of variable cost, most of it electricity. Operating cost alone is $2.77 per kilogram. What the hydrogen has to sell for depends on how you charge for the $400 million, and the four honest ways of doing it give anything from $3.21 to $4.68 a kilogram. The lowest number divides the capital by the plant life and stops. The highest builds a year-by-year after-tax cash flow and asks what price earns a 10 % return. Everything between is a shortcut to that cash flow, and most of this lesson is about where the difference comes from and which number to quote. I keep doing these estimates by hand and checking them against my own toolkit, so every number on this page is computed rather than copied. You can open the same plant in the techno-economic analysis tool and change any of it. The worked example Illustrative, not a design. Capital $400 M overnight, 3-year build, 30-year life. Fixed O&M $18 M/yr, variable $65 M/yr: about 50 kWh/kg at 4.3 ¢/kWh. 10 % real after-tax return, 25.74 % tax, MACRS 7-year depreciation. Levelised cost is the constant price, per unit of product, that recovers every cost including a return on capital. When it is solved from a cash flow at NPV = 0 it is called the minimum selling price (MSP). 01

A techno-economic analysis (TEA) joins a process design to a cash flow. It answers three questions in order: what the plant costs to build, what it costs to run, and what the product must sell for to pay back both with a return. A fourth question usually follows: at the market price, is the investment worth making? The answer is only as good as the least certain input, and that is almost always the capital at the screening stage. AACE International classifies estimates by how much of the engineering is done. A TEA built from cost correlations and factors sits at Class 5 or Class 4, which is why it is a tool for comparing options and finding what matters, not a budget. Table 1. AACE estimate classes for the process industries Class Definition complete Typical use Low range High range 5 0–2 % Concept screening −20 to −50 % +30 to +100 % 4 1–15 % Study or feasibility −15 to −30 % +20 to +50 % 3 10–40 % Budget authorisation −10 to −20 % +10 to +30 % 2 30–75 % Control or bid −5 to −15 % +5 to +20 % 1 65–100 % Check estimate or bid −3 to −10 % +3 to +15 % Source: AACE International Recommended Practice 18R-97 (2011 revision). Ranges are at about 80 % confidence; each class spans the values given, depending on the technology and the estimator. The ranges are asymmetric: early estimates are more often too low than too high, so the high side is wider. Keep that in mind every time a number below has three significant figures: the third figure is arithmetic, not knowledge. Nth plant. The national-lab convention, used here, assumes several plants of the same design already run, so there is no first-of-a-kind premium. For a first commercial unit an nth-plant number is a floor, not an estimate. Rule of thumb. If two options differ by less than the estimate range, the TEA has not chosen between them. It has told you which inputs to firm up first. 02

Equipment cost rises more slowly than capacity. A vessel's capacity grows with its volume and its cost with its wall area, so doubling the size does not double the price. The standard correlation is a power law in the size that drives cost, such as heat-transfer area, flow or volume: C₂ = C₁ (S₂ / S₁)ⁿ (1) With nothing better, n = 0.6, the six-tenths rule. Individual equipment types scatter from about 0.3 to 1.0, so use a fitted exponent when one exists. The DOE/NETL report by Loh, Lyons and White tabulates cost against size for 31 kinds of equipment on a 1998 US Gulf Coast basis, and fitting those points gives exponents with known quality. For a shell-and-tube exchanger, carbon steel, 150 psig, the fit is $66,278 at 3,455 ft² with n = 0.708, from 26 points over 100–70,000 ft², R² = 0.95. A usable cost needs three more corrections: the dollar-year, the material and the location. C = C₁ (S/S₁)ⁿ × (CEPCI_now / CEPCI_base) × F_M × F_L (2) For a 5,000 ft² exchanger the power law gives $86,094 in 1998 dollars. The Chemical Engineering Plant Cost Index was 389.5 in 1998, and my provisional estimate for 2025 is 810.3, a ratio of 2.08, so the exchanger costs $179,106 in 2025. In 316 stainless, with a material factor of 2.9 for static equipment, it is $519,406. Rotating machinery takes a smaller alloy penalty (1.8 for a 316 pump) because less of its cost is wetted metal. CEPCI is a composite price index for chemical plant construction, published monthly by Chemical Engineering . Cost engineers prefer to escalate over five years or less; 1998 to 2025 is 27, which widens the error band on its own. Size outside the fit. Below the fitted range, a power law is extrapolation. Above the largest shop-fabricable unit, cost becomes linear: you buy several units, not one bigger one. Two things in Figure 2 are worth noticing. The six-tenths rule, drawn through the same 5,000 ft² point, underestimates a 20,000 ft² exchanger by 14 % because the real exponent is 0.708. And past 70,000 ft² the curve bends upward: 150,000 ft² is costed as three parallel exchangers of 50,000 ft² each, $2.74 million, rather than one imaginary exchanger at the extrapolated price. Quietly extrapolating a power law past the largest unit a vendor can build is one of the commonest ways to underestimate a large plant. 03

A purchased exchanger sitting on a truck is a small part of what it costs to have it working. Foundations, steel, piping, instruments, electrical, insulation, paint and the labour to install all of them typically make purchased equipment only 15–30 % of the finished plant. There are three ways to add them, in increasing order of effort.

entries.h: One factor for the whole plant
entries.x: Lang's 1948 factors multiply delivered equipment cost by 3.10 for a solids plant, 3.63 for solids and fluids, and 4.74 for fluid processing. They are quick and blunt, good to perhaps ±30–50 %.

The DOE/NETL method builds the installation from bulk materials, each a fraction of the bare equipment cost, and the labour to install each bulk as a fraction of that material. The fractions depend on service: gas or liquid, temperature above or below 400 °F, pressure above or below 150 psig. Table 2 reproduces the worked example in the report, a gas-to-gas exchanger with a bare cost of $62,000. Table 2. Installed cost of a $62,000 exchanger by distributive factors Gas service above 400 °F and below 150 psig; setting labour 20 % of equipment for a heat exchanger. Factors and the $150,245 result from Loh, Lyons and White (2002), Tables 5–6 and Appendix A. The installed cost is 2.42 times the bare cost. Piping is the largest single bulk, which is typical of fluid plants and is why the distributive factors for a gas plant run higher than for solids handling. The same method can be applied with one service class for the whole plant or with a class per item; the second is more work and gives a pump and a crusher different factors, which they deserve.

entries.h: A factor from a similar plant
entries.x: If you have a completed project of similar type, its installed-to-purchased ratio beats both. Record where it came from. Bare erected cost (BEC) is the result: equipment, bulks and installation labour, plus on-site facilities. It is the first rung of the capital ladder in section 04. Quoted installed prices , such as an electrolyser stack priced per kilowatt installed, go into BEC directly. Never multiply an installed price by an installation factor, and never add purchased and installed costs in one subtotal. 04

NETL's cost methodology defines five capital levels, each built on the last. The names matter, because published capital numbers are quoted at different rungs and the gap between them is large. EPCC = BEC × (1 + f_EPC) TPC = EPCC + process contingency + project contingency TOC = TPC + owner’s costs TASC = TOC × (TASC/TOC) (3) EPC cost adds the engineering, procurement and construction contractor's services, 15–20 % of BEC. Total plant cost adds contingency. Process contingency covers an immature technology (0–10 % when commercial, 20–35 % from pilot data, more from the bench). Project contingency covers what a budget estimate leaves out, 15–30 % of BEC plus EPC plus process contingency. Total overnight cost adds owner's costs: pre-production 2 % of TPC, spare parts 0.5 %, financing fees 2.7 %, other owner's costs 15 % (studies, permitting, legal, owner's engineering), plus land. Total as-spent capital adds escalation and the cost of carrying the money through construction. It is in mixed, as-spent dollars; the other four are overnight costs in the dollars of one base year. TOC or TASC? Always ask which one a published number is. Multiplying a fixed charge rate by TOC instead of TASC understates the capital charge by 9 % for a three-year build in real terms, and by about 24 % in nominal terms. The TASC/TOC factor comes from the spend profile. Money committed in year n of a y-year build sits in the project for y − n + 1 years before the plant earns anything, accruing simple interest at the pre-tax weighted cost of capital: TASC/TOC = Σₙ (1+e)ⁿ⁻¹ pₙ + Σₙ WACC (y−n+1)(1+e)ⁿ⁻¹ pₙ (4) For NETL's three-year gas-plant profile (10, 60 and 30 % of TOC by year), a 5.14 % real WACC and no real escalation, the factor is 1 + 0.0514 × (3 × 0.1 + 2 × 0.6 + 1 × 0.3) = 1.0925. Table 3. TASC/TOC factors under NETL assumptions Build Basis WACC Escalation TASC/TOC 3 years Real 5.14 % 0 % 1.093 5 years Real 5.14 % 0 % 1.154 3 years Nominal 7.25 % 3 % 1.242 5 years Nominal 7.25 % 3 % 1.289 Computed from equation (4) with NETL-PUB-22580 spend profiles; the nominal three-year case starts its spend two years after the base year, as NETL does, which is why it carries extra escalation. All four match NETL's published values. 05

Split operating cost the way an operator would. Variable cost scales with output: feeds, catalysts and chemicals, utilities, waste disposal. Fixed cost is incurred whether or not the plant runs: labour, maintenance, insurance and local tax, overhead. For many chemical plants the levelised cost is dominated by one or two variable lines, and a capital estimate good to −30/+50 % on top of a feed price guessed to a factor of two is not a Class 4 estimate of anything. Variable lines are rate × hours × capacity factor × price. Put consumption at full rate and let the capacity factor scale it, so changing the operating time moves every line together.

Turton's correlation gives operators needed at any moment from the process configuration, where P counts steps handling particulate solids and N np counts compressors, towers, reactors, heaters and exchangers: N_OL = (6.29 + 31.7 P² + 0.23 N_np)^0.5 (5) Twelve non-particulate steps need 3.0 operators per shift; add two solids-handling steps and it rises to 11.7, which says something true about solids. A seat staffed around the clock takes 4.5 to 5 people once holidays, leave and training are counted.

Fixed-cost conventions come as sets, and each set assumes what is inside its lines. NREL's biorefinery reports charge a 90 % labour burden on salaries, and that 90 % already covers benefits and payroll overhead. Peters and Timmerhaus's plant overhead includes payroll overhead too. If you add a 35 % benefits burden to salaries first and then apply either overhead, you count benefits twice and take the overhead on the inflated figure. Four operators a shift, $78,000 salary, 25 % supervision Salaries: 4 × 4.8 × 78,000 × 1.25 = $1,872,000. NREL: × 1.90 = $3,556,800 . Burden added first, then the 90 %: 1,872,000 + 524,160 burden, × 1.90 = $4,552,704, which is 28 % too high . I found exactly this in an earlier version of my own toolkit, which is why I mention it. Pick one convention, read what its lines contain, and do not add anything it already includes. Table 4. Three fixed-cost conventions Line NREL Peters & Timmerhaus NETL Maintenance 3 % of installed cost 5 % of FCI 2 % of TPC Insurance and local tax 0.7 % of FCI 2 % of FCI 2 % of TPC Labour charged as Salaries Salaries Loaded (with burden) Overhead 90 % of salaries 60 % of labour + maintenance 30 % of labour Administration in the 90 % 20 % of labour + maintenance 25 % of labour Laboratory, supplies — 15 % of labour; 15 % of maintenance — NREL/TP-5100-47764 §5; Peters, Timmerhaus and West, 5th ed., ch. 6 midpoints; NETL-PUB-22580 §4. FCI here is fixed capital investment, taken as TOC.

Turton's one-line cost of manufacture absorbs maintenance, overhead and administration into three multipliers. It is a good check on a line-by-line build-up; if the two disagree by more than about 20 %, one of them is wrong. COM_d = 0.180 FCI + 2.73 C_OL + 1.23 (C_UT + C_WT + C_RM) (6) For a $100 million plant with $2.5 million of operating labour and $45 million of utilities, waste and raw materials, COM d is $80.2 million a year. Not operating costs. Depreciation and interest belong to the costing method in sections 06 and 07, never to operating cost. Charging depreciation in operating cost and again through the discount rate is the commonest single error in a first TEA. Capacity factor is output relative to nameplate while running. Operating hours are time on stream. Keep them separate so a turndown and an outage are not the same input. 06

Capital is spent before the product is sold, and someone has to be paid for waiting. The capital recovery factor (CRF) is the annual payment that repays one dollar over N years at rate r, the same arithmetic as a mortgage: CRF = r (1+r)ᴺ / [ (1+r)ᴺ − 1 ] (7) At 10 % over 30 years CRF is 0.1061, so the hydrogen plant's $400 million costs $42.4 million a year to own before tax, against $13.3 million if you divide by the life. That gap is the whole difference between $3.21 and $4.18 per kilogram in Figure 1. Income tax adds to it. Revenue that repays capital is taxed, but depreciation is deductible. The fixed charge rate (FCR) grosses the capital recovery up for tax and gives back the present value of the depreciation shield, where dₙ is the depreciation fraction in year n: FCR = CRF/(1−t) − t · CRF · Σₙ dₙ/(1+r)ⁿ / (1−t) (8) With NETL's after-tax WACC of 4.73 % real, 30 years, a 25.74 % tax rate and 20-year MACRS depreciation, FCR = 0.0707; at 6.54 % nominal it is 0.0885. NETL publishes 0.0707 and 0.0886, the same to rounding. NETL charges the FCR against TASC, not TOC.

A real analysis uses constant dollars of one year and a real discount rate. A nominal analysis inflates every cost and uses a nominal rate. The two rates are linked by the Fisher relation: (1 + r_nominal) = (1 + r_real)(1 + i) (9) NETL's 7.25 % nominal WACC is 5.14 % real at 2.01 % inflation. Applying a nominal rate to cash flows that do not inflate overstates the cost; applying a real rate to inflating ones understates it. In a nominal formula method, operating cost that escalates at i is levelised with a factor that NETL gives as 1.384 for 3 % escalation over 30 years at 6.54 %: LF = CRF × [ 1 − ((1+i)/(1+r))ᴺ ] / (r − i) (10) MACRS is the US tax depreciation schedule (IRS Publication 946). NREL uses the 7-year class for general plant and NETL the 20-year class for power plants. The faster the schedule, the larger the present value of the tax shield and the lower the FCR. WACC is the weighted average cost of capital: the share of equity times its required return plus the share of debt times its interest. The after-tax WACC deducts tax on the interest. 07

entries.h: The cash flow and the minimum selling price
entries.x: The formula methods are approximations of one thing: an after-tax cash flow, year by year, from the first dollar of construction to the end of life, solved for the product price at which the net present value is zero at the required return. NREL calls the result the minimum selling price, and it is what US national-lab studies report. Σₜ [ P·Qₜ + Bₜ − OPEXₜ − Taxₜ − Capitalₜ ] / (1+r)ᵗ = 0 → solve for P Taxₜ = t × (P·Qₜ + Bₜ − OPEXₜ − Depreciationₜ − Interestₜ) (11) The cash flow carries what the formulas cannot: Capital spent over the build, here 8, 60 and 32 % of TOC over three years, the NREL profile. A start-up year at half revenue but 75 % of variable cost and all of fixed cost. Depreciation on the actual schedule, and tax losses in early years carried forward against later profit. Working capital spent at start-up and recovered at the end; land bought, never depreciated, and recovered at the end. Debt drawn during construction accruing interest until the plant starts, then repaid in level payments. IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV zero for a given price. At the minimum selling price the IRR equals the required return, by construction. A check worth running. With no tax, a one-year build and no start-up penalty, the cash flow gives exactly the CRF answer, $4.18/kg. With tax, and losses credited in the year they occur, it gives exactly the FCR answer. If your spreadsheet does not, something in it is wrong. At 10 % the hydrogen has to sell for $4.68 a kilogram, of which $2.77 is operating cost and $1.91 is the capital charge, including tax. That is more than the FCR's $4.59 because the cash flow compounds the cost of carrying construction spend where TASC adds it as simple interest, loses half a year of revenue at start-up, and defers tax deductions it cannot use yet. Each two points on the discount rate move the price by 32 to 39 cents. If the hydrogen actually sells for $5.50, the same cash flow gives an NPV of $140 million at 10 %, an IRR of 14.1 % and a discounted payback in operating year 11.4.

entries.h: Three errors the cash flow makes easy
entries.x: When I audited my own toolkit against these rules I found three, and they are worth checking in any model: Land depreciated. NETL puts land inside TOC, so a model that depreciates TOC depreciates land, and if land is also entered as its own outflow it is paid for twice. Depreciate TOC less land. A nominal rate on real cash flows. Choosing a nominal basis must inflate costs, not only change the discount rate. Free construction debt. Debt drawn during a three-year build accrues interest before the first repayment. A useful test: with no tax, borrowing at exactly the discount rate must leave the selling price unchanged. If leverage makes the product cheaper in that test, the loan is being given away. 08

Most plants make more than one thing: export steam, surplus power, oxygen from an electrolyser. The simplest treatment credits byproduct revenue against cost and charges the rest to the main product. It is the right choice when the byproduct is small. When credits approach half of total cost, the main product's cost becomes a small difference of large numbers, and the headline is really a forecast of the byproduct price. Then allocate cost between co-products by mass, energy content or market value instead, and say which. The choice can move the answer by a factor of two, and a levelised cost that does not name its allocation rule cannot be reproduced.

A production credit pays a fixed amount per unit made, for a fixed number of years: per kilogram of low-carbon hydrogen, per tonne of CO 2 stored. Two things decide what it is worth to the selling price. It stops partway through the life, so it has to be discounted over its own years and then spread over the whole life. And if it arrives as untaxed cash, as a tax credit taken by direct pay or sold to another taxpayer usually does, a dollar of credit is worth more than a dollar of taxable revenue: K_lev = K × Σ_{y=1..Y} 1/(1+r)ʸ × CRF(r, N) / (1 − t) ÷ Q (12) Drop the (1 − t) when the credit is taxed as income. For the hydrogen plant, a credit of $3/kg for ten years is worth $2.63/kg in the formula and takes the cash-flow selling price from $4.68 to $2.55/kg as untaxed cash, or to $2.75/kg if it were taxed. The cash flow gives back less than the formula because the lower price pushes the early years into tax losses and defers the depreciation shield. A credit that large deserves the same warning as a large byproduct: quote the cost with and without it, because the credit can be withdrawn, can expire before the plant does, and usually has eligibility rules that a TEA cannot check. A quick test. Raise every byproduct price by 10 % and see how far the main product's cost moves. An elasticity above about 1.5 means the byproduct market, not the process, is setting the answer. US credits, as of late 2026. The clean hydrogen credit (45V) pays up to $3/kg for ten years but now only for facilities that begin construction before 2028. The carbon storage credit (45Q) pays $85/t of CO 2 for twelve years when prevailing-wage rules are met. Check the current rules before relying on either. Canada supports hydrogen and carbon capture mainly through investment tax credits on capital, which reduce TOC rather than paying per unit. 09

A single levelised cost is less useful than knowing which three inputs it depends on. A tornado chart moves one input at a time between a low and a high value and ranks the swings. Use ranges that reflect how well each kind of input is known: capital at the class range, commodity prices at ±30 %, consumption from a converged flowsheet at ±10 %, capacity factor from −10 to +3 % because plants rarely beat nameplate. A flat ±20 % on everything is the commonest way to draw a misleading tornado. For the range of outcomes rather than the ranking, sample every uncertain input at once (Monte Carlo) and report P10, P50 and P90, with the input distributions stated. And to turn the question round, solve for the input that hits a target: what electricity price gives hydrogen at $3 a kilogram? That break-even is often the most useful sentence in the report. The tool linked below draws the tornado for whatever plant you enter, and the desktop toolkit adds Monte Carlo and break-even solving. 10

Name the costing method, the discount rate, real or nominal, the tax rate and the dollar-year in the same sentence as the number. Say whether capital is TOC or TASC, and charge a fixed charge rate only against TASC. Check that depreciation and interest appear nowhere in operating cost. Read what your fixed-cost convention already contains before adding burden, overhead or administration. Look for equipment sized outside its correlation range, and for installed quotes multiplied by an installation factor. Run all four methods. If straight-line is close to the cash flow, the discount rate is near zero or the capital is negligible; if the FCR is far from the cash flow, the tax or depreciation assumptions differ. Report the estimate class and the three inputs that move the answer most. For a first-of-a-kind plant, say that the result is an nth-plant floor. Try it on your own plant The tool runs this whole lesson on any equipment list: the correlations, the capital ladder, the four methods, the cash flow and the tornado, with the working shown and every figure downloadable. Two-phase gas–liquid separators Flash drums, knockout drums and scrubbers: how to choose the type, size a vertical or horizontal vessel, pick the internals, read mist-eliminator and packaged-separator vendor data, apply ASME, API 12J and API 521, and keep liquid out of places it should never reach. Nine worked examples and sixteen problems to solve. Alireza Lotfollahzade , EIT Updated 15 November 2026 About 100 minutes to read, longer with the problems SI units; vendor figures are quoted from published sheets, model curves are illustrative Figure 1. The gas sets a vertical separator’s diameter; the liquid sets its height Mist eliminator Service Presets Gas flow Pressure Temperature Gas molar mass Gas compressibility, Z Liquid flow Liquid density Holdup time, NLL to LALL Surge time, NLL to LAHH – m/s Allowable gas velocity, K√((ρ L −ρ G )/ρ G ) – mm Inside diameter – mm Height, tangent to tangent – Height to diameter ratio Band, bottom to top Height, mm Sizing by the method in sections 05 and 06: Souders–Brown with GPSA mesh-pad K values derated for pressure, half of that without a mist eliminator, 0.15 m/s for an upflow vane pack and 0.20 m/s for an axial-cyclone deck (both derated the same way); 100 mm added for the support ring and the diameter rounded up in 150 mm steps; the diameter is increased until height ÷ diameter is 4 or less. Nozzles: inlet ρv² ≤ 2,100 Pa with a half-open pipe, gas outlet ρv² ≤ 3,750 Pa, liquid outlet ≤ 1 m/s. Gas density from pV = ZnRT. Heads are 2:1 ellipsoidal and their volume is ignored. Illustrative screening only; the vendor and the vessel designer finish the job. A separator is the plainest-looking vessel on a P&ID and one of the most consequential. When it fails, liquid ends up in a compressor, a fuel-gas header or a flare, and gas ends up in a vessel that was never designed for it. This page is written for chemical and process engineers who size drums, review vendor proposals and sit in HAZOPs. Figure 1 is the whole method in one place: the gas flow and the K-factor fix the diameter, the liquid flow and the holdup and surge times fix the height, and the nozzles and internals fill in the rest. Try the Example 3 preset: there is so much liquid that the drum has to be made wider than the gas needs, and then the mesh pad is too big for the gas flowing through it. The sections below explain every step behind that figure, then go further into horizontal vessels, internals, vendor data, mechanical design, standards and safety. If you can solve the problems at the end without opening the solutions, you can specify and check most two-phase separators you will meet. After this page you can Run a flash, size vertical and horizontal separators, choose K and internals, size nozzles, read mist-eliminator and packaged-separator data sheets, calculate shell thickness to ASME VIII, estimate fire and gas-blowby relief loads, and name the safeguards a HAZOP will ask for. 01

A two-phase separator takes a stream that is part gas and part liquid and sends each phase out of its own nozzle, with as little of the other phase as the downstream equipment can tolerate. Whatever the orientation, it does this in four zones, which the GPSA Engineering Data Book labels A to D. 1 A, the inlet or primary section. An inlet device absorbs the momentum of the feed and drops out most of the liquid as bulk liquid. A good inlet device also spreads the gas evenly across the vessel. A bad one shatters liquid into fine mist that nothing downstream can catch. B, the gravity settling section. The gas slows down and droplets fall out under gravity. It is usually sized so that droplets of about 100–150 µm and larger settle before the gas reaches the mist eliminator. 7 12 C, the mist extraction section. A mesh pad, vane pack or bank of cyclones catches the fine droplets, down to around 10 µm or smaller, by impaction and coalescence. 6 8 D, the liquid collection section. The liquid gives up its entrained gas bubbles, and the volume between the level settings gives the control system and the operators time to react. Most sizing arguments are about which of these zones runs out of room first. In a scrubber with a little condensate, it is the gas zones B and C. In a flash drum taking a large liquid flow, it is zone D. Flash drum, knockout drum, scrubber. The names overlap. A flash drum receives a liquid that partly vaporizes on entry; a knockout drum or scrubber removes a small amount of liquid from a mostly gas stream. The sizing method is the same. Figure 2. Vertical and horizontal separators have the same four zones in a different arrangement Schematic, not to scale. Left: a vertical separator with a half-open-pipe inlet and a horizontal mesh pad. Right: a horizontal separator with an inlet deflector and a vane pack in horizontal gas flow. Red dashed lines are the high-high and low-low trip levels. Zone letters follow the GPSA convention. 1

The liquid zone is defined by its level settings. From the bottom up they are usually the low-low trip (LALL), the low alarm (LAL), the normal level (NLL), the high alarm (LAH) and the high-high trip (LAHH). Svrcek and Monnery give the definitions most sizing procedures use: 2 Holdup is the time for the level to fall from normal to the low-low level at the normal outlet flow with no feed. It protects whatever the liquid goes to next, such as a pump, a column or a heater. Surge is the time for the level to rise from normal to the high-high level at the normal feed rate with the outlet closed. It absorbs slugs and upsets. Without a better basis, Svrcek and Monnery take surge as half the holdup time. Some companies measure surge between the low and high levels instead. Which definition you use matters less than writing it on the data sheet so the vendor sizes the same volume you did. Tag names vary. API RP 14C calls the shutdown sensors LSH and LSL; many P&IDs use LAHH and LALL, or HHLL and LLLL. Check the legend sheet before comparing two designs. 02

entries.h: Types and where they are used

entries.x: Vertical separators are the usual choice when the gas-to-liquid ratio is high or the total gas flow is modest, as in scrubbers and knockout drums. 1 They need less plot space, which matters offshore, and they make solids easier to remove from the bottom head. 15 A given change in liquid volume also moves the level further, which makes level control and trips more responsive. Their weakness is that droplets must fall against the rising gas, so the full cross-section is limited by the settling velocity. Horizontal separators win when there is a lot of liquid, when the liquid foams or carries dissolved gas that needs a large surface to escape, when slugs arrive, or when a second liquid phase must also settle. Droplets fall across the gas flow rather than against it, so for the same flow area a horizontal drum can run at a higher gas velocity than a vertical one. 33 The cost is plot space and a level that moves less for a given volume change. Spherical separators are compact and strong, but they have little surge volume and are hard to fit with internals. They are rare in new plants and are outside the scope of API RP 12J. 4 A quick screen. Run Figure 1 for your duty. If the height-to-diameter ratio comes out above about 5 even after widening, or the liquid holdup is several cubic metres, price a horizontal drum as well.

Flash drum A liquid enters below its bubble point downstream of a let-down valve or a heater and partly vaporizes. Examples are amine and glycol flash tanks, hot and cold high-pressure separators in hydrotreaters, and stage separators in gas plants. Vertical or horizontal, usually with a mesh pad. The feed nozzle sees flashing two-phase flow. Knockout drum Removes free liquid and condensate from a gas: fuel-gas knockout drums, upstream of burners and gas turbines, ahead of meters and analysers. Vertical, with a mesh pad or vane pack. Compressor suction scrubber The last line of defence for a compressor. Liquid slugs break valves in reciprocating machines and erode impellers in centrifugal ones, so the scrubber has a conservative K and a high-high level trip that stops the compressor. Vertical, mesh pad, vane pack or cyclones. GPSA multiplies K by 0.7–0.8 for this service. 1 Inlet, production and test separators Separate well fluids into gas and liquid in oil and gas fields. Test separators measure the rates from one well at a time. Usually horizontal. API RP 12J and API Spec 12J cover them. 4 5 Reflux drum or overhead accumulator Collects condensed distillation overhead, supplies reflux and product, and vents non-condensables. Often carries a water boot. Horizontal; the holdup is usually set on the reflux flow. 28 Flare knockout drum Removes liquid from relief and blowdown streams so the flare does not rain burning liquid. Sized for droplets of 300–600 µm and 20–30 minutes of holdup for the largest liquid release. 24 Usually horizontal, no internals. Covered by API 521, not API RP 12J. 4 16 Slug catcher Receives liquid slugs at the end of a multiphase pipeline. Above about 35 bar, a manifold of large pipes (a finger-type slug catcher) is often cheaper than one thick-walled vessel. 34 Vessel type or finger type; sized on the largest expected slug volume. Steam drum and evaporator separator Separates steam from boiler water, or vapour from a boiling liquor. Steam purity sets the design, so high-efficiency mesh is common. Horizontal steam drums; vertical evaporator bodies. 8 Filter separator and coalescer Removes submicron aerosols that a mesh pad cannot, ahead of membranes, amine contactors, turboexpanders and gas turbines. Filter elements followed by a vane section. Outside API RP 12J. 4 Compact and inline cyclonic separators Use swirl instead of gravity to save weight and space, mostly offshore and in debottlenecks. Proprietary designs, sized by the vendor. Outside API RP 12J. 4 03

entries.h: The flash: what arrives at the separator
entries.x: A separator does not decide how much gas and liquid it receives. Thermodynamics does, and the separator only decides how cleanly they part. In design the vapour and liquid rates, compositions and densities come from a flash calculation, usually in a simulator. It is still worth being able to do one by hand, because a hand flash is how you catch a wrong thermodynamic package, a missing component or a feed entered on the wrong basis. For an isothermal flash of F kmol/h of feed with mole fractions z i into V kmol/h of vapour and L of liquid, with equilibrium ratios K i = y i /x i , the vapour fraction β = V/F is the root of the Rachford–Rice equation: Σ z i (K i − 1) / [1 + β(K i − 1)] = 0 (1) x i = z i / [1 + β(K i − 1)] y i = K i x i (2) The left side of (1) falls steadily as β goes from 0 to 1. If it is positive at β = 1, the feed is all vapour; if it is negative at β = 0, it is all liquid. Otherwise there is exactly one root between them, which a few bisection steps will find. For a quick estimate of K at low to moderate pressure, the Wilson correlation uses only critical properties and the acentric factor: K i ≈ (p c,i /p) exp[5.373 (1 + ω i )(1 − T c,i /T)] (3) A drum downstream of a let-down valve is an adiabatic flash: the feed enthalpy is conserved, so the drum temperature is found by adjusting T until the vapour and liquid enthalpies, weighted by β, equal the feed enthalpy. That temperature drop is how separators downstream of choke and let-down valves end up cold enough to form hydrates or to need impact-tested steel. Example 1 in section 12 runs a six-component flash by hand. Its vapour and liquid rates feed Examples 2 to 8. Use Wilson for checking, not design. It ignores composition and is poor near the critical point. A cubic equation of state such as Peng–Robinson is the normal basis for hydrocarbon separators. Size for every case. Summer and winter, start-of-life and end-of-life, turndown and upset. The case that sets the diameter is often not the one that sets the height. 04

A droplet of diameter d in a rising gas feels its weight less buoyancy pulling it down, and drag pushing it up. It stops accelerating when they balance, at its terminal velocity: (π d³/6)(ρ L − ρ G ) g = C D (π d²/4) ρ G v t ²/2 (4) v t = √[ 4 g d (ρ L − ρ G ) / (3 C D ρ G ) ] (5) The drag coefficient C D depends on the droplet Reynolds number Re = ρ G v t d / μ G , so (5) is solved by iteration. A smooth-sphere correlation that covers the whole range up to Re ≈ 2 × 10⁵ is Turton and Levenspiel’s: 22 C D = (24/Re)(1 + 0.173 Re 0.657 ) + 0.413 / (1 + 16,300 Re −1.09 ) (6) Two limits are useful. At Re below about 1, C D = 24/Re and (5) becomes Stokes’ law, v t = g d² (ρ L − ρ G ) / (18 μ G ): velocity rises with the square of the diameter. At Re above about 1,000, C D is close to 0.44 and velocity rises only with the square root of the diameter. Most droplets in process separators fall between the two. Rearranging (5) shows where the Souders–Brown equation comes from: v t = K √[(ρ L − ρ G )/ρ G ] with K = √[ 4 g d / (3 C D ) ] (7) K has units of velocity and carries the droplet size and the drag. For a separator without a mist eliminator, K is a statement about which droplet size you are willing to let through. For a separator with a mist eliminator, K is an empirical limit on the device, set by re-entrainment and flooding, and droplet physics no longer sets it directly. Design droplet sizes. About 100–150 µm for a gravity section ahead of a mist eliminator, 300–600 µm for flare knockout drums, and 10 µm and below for the mist eliminator itself. 7 24 6 Droplets are not spheres of one size. Real inlet streams carry a distribution of sizes set mainly by the inlet piping and inlet device. That is why the inlet momentum limits in section 08 matter as much as K. Figure 3. At 39 barg a 150 µm droplet falls at 0.16 m/s; in air at 1 atm it falls almost three times faster Droplet diameter 150 µm – m/s Terminal velocity – Droplet Reynolds number – Drag coefficient, equation (6) – m/s Equivalent K, equation (7) Hydrocarbon case: ρ G = 35.3 kg/m³, ρ L = 620 kg/m³, μ G = 0.012 mPa·s, the conditions of Example 2. Air and water: ρ G = 1.20, ρ L = 998 kg/m³, μ G = 0.0181 mPa·s. Drag from Turton and Levenspiel. 22 Stokes’ law overestimates the velocity of large droplets badly. Shaded bands: 100–150 µm (gravity section ahead of a mist eliminator) and 300–600 µm (flare knockout drums). Two numbers from Figure 3 are worth remembering. At the hydrocarbon conditions, the GPSA K for a vertical drum without a mist eliminator (half of 0.093, or 0.047 m/s) corresponds to a droplet of about 180 µm. The mesh-pad K of 0.093 m/s corresponds to about 390 µm. So a vertical drum running at its mesh-pad limit carries droplets of several hundred microns up to the pad, and the pad, not gravity, does most of the work. That is why the mist eliminator is sized so carefully, and why it is the first thing to check when a drum carries over. 05

entries.h: The K-factor and the Souders–Brown equation
entries.x: The Souders–Brown equation gives the maximum allowable gas velocity, and with it the minimum flow area: V max = K √[(ρ L − ρ G )/ρ G ] A min = Q G / V max (8) Q G is the actual gas flow at separator conditions (m³/s), not a standard flow. A is the full cross-section of a vertical vessel, or the face area of the mist eliminator. The equation is simple; choosing K is the engineering. The values below are the starting points used in industry. They are for clean, non-foaming systems and for the mist eliminators described, and they assume a reasonable inlet device and an even gas distribution. Units. K in m/s here; 1 ft/s = 0.3048 m/s, so the classic 0.35 ft/s is 0.107 m/s. Some companies call the term √(ρ G /(ρ L −ρ G )) × V the “load factor”. It is the same K. Table 1. GPSA K for vertical drums with a horizontal mesh pad. The Souders–Brown equation already lowers the velocity as gas density rises, so the extra derating in Table 1 can look like double counting. It is not. As pressure rises the gas-to-liquid density ratio rises and the surface tension falls, so droplets are smaller, break up more easily and are re-entrained from wet surfaces at lower velocities. Campbell attributes the decline of mesh pad K with pressure mainly to these two effects. 7

High liquid load to the mist eliminator. Above about 0.75 US gpm/ft² (1.8 m³/m²·h) for a standard mesh pad, Campbell reduces K by 10 % for each additional 1 gpm/ft² (2.4 m³/m²·h). 7 Foaming or low surface tension : glycol, amine, some crudes and condensates near their critical point. Fouling, wax or solids : use a lower K with an open mesh, or a vane pack, and plan for cleaning. Slugs and surges : vendors apply a derating factor for these exceptional conditions. 8 The opposite mistake is just as real. A mesh pad needs enough velocity for droplets to hit the wires. Below roughly a quarter of its design velocity it loses efficiency, and droplets pass straight through. 8 A scrubber sized for a future flow can therefore carry over today. Which K is the vendor quoting? A vane K at the vane face can be 0.45 m/s while the same vessel’s cross-section runs at 0.15 m/s. Always ask what area a K refers to. 06
This is the procedure behind Figure 1. It follows Svrcek and Monnery’s method with GPSA K values, which is still the most common hand method in process design offices. 2 1

entries.h: Step 1. Gas and liquid at separator conditions
entries.x: Convert every flow to actual volume at the separator’s pressure and temperature. For the gas, ρ G = p M / (Z R T) Q G = ṁ G / ρ G (9) p in Pa absolute, M in kg/kmol, R = 8,314 J/(kmol·K), T in K. Take Z from the same equation of state as the flash.

Pick K from Tables 1 and 2, derate it for pressure and service, and find V max from equation (8). The mist-eliminator diameter follows, and the vessel is made slightly larger to leave room for the support ring: D ME = √(4 Q G / (π V max )) D ≥ D ME + 75 to 150 mm (10) Svrcek and Monnery add 3–6 in and round up to the next 6 in (about 150 mm). 3 Without a mist eliminator the whole cross-section is the gravity section and no ring allowance is needed.

entries.x: h H = t H Q L / A h S = t S Q L / A (11) Holdup and surge times are set by what the liquid goes to and how good the control is. Table 3 gives the usual starting points. Volumes in the heads. Hand methods usually ignore the liquid in the bottom head, which gives a little extra margin. Include it when you are rating an existing vessel and every minute counts. Table 3. entries.h: Step 5. Add up and check the proportions
entries.x: H TT = h LALL + h H + h S + h in + h D + h ME + h top (12) Vertical two-phase separators usually end up with a height-to-diameter ratio of about 3 to 5. 12 If H/D is well above that, the liquid is controlling: increase the diameter, which shortens the liquid column, and repeat. If H/D is below about 2, the fixed spacings are controlling and the vessel is about as small as it can be. Widening a vessel for liquid has a side effect that catches people out. The gas velocity in a full-diameter mesh pad falls, sometimes below its turndown limit. The fix is to keep the pad sized for the gas: either a full-diameter pad with an annular blanking plate, or a smaller pad in a box around the gas outlet. 12 Figure 1 does this automatically when the velocity in a full-diameter device falls below about 25 % of design for mesh (30 % for cyclones, 40 % for vanes). Example 3 works through it.

Size the nozzles from section 08, check the inlet nozzle against the height you allowed for it, then pass the vessel to mechanical design (section 10). Why 0.5 D? The gas leaving the inlet device needs a vertical distance to spread across the vessel before it reaches the mist eliminator. A wide vessel needs more height to even out the flow. Don’t hide the trip levels. Show LALL, LAL, NLL, LAH and LAHH as heights above the bottom tangent on the data sheet, with the times they represent. 07

In a horizontal drum the gas flows along the vessel above the liquid, and a droplet released at the top must fall through the gas space before the gas carries it to the outlet. The cross-section is shared, so every calculation needs the area of a circular segment. For a liquid depth h in a drum of diameter D, the fraction of the cross-section below the liquid surface is f(h/D) = (θ − sin θ) / (2π) with θ = 2 arccos(1 − 2h/D) (13) θ in radians. At h/D = 0.5, f = 0.5; at h/D = 0.25, f = 0.196. The gas area above a level is A T [1 − f(h/D)].

Svrcek and Monnery’s method, in SI units: 2 Find the settling velocity with a no-mist-eliminator K (half the GPSA value), and use 75 % of it, U V = 0.75 U T , for a conservative design. Calculate the holdup and surge volumes, V H = t H Q L and V S = t S Q L . Guess L/D and get a first diameter, assuming holdup and surge fill about 60 % of the drum: D = [ 4(V H + V S ) / (0.6 π (L/D)) ] 1/3 (14) Set the low-low level. Svrcek and Monnery use 0.5 D(ft) + 7 in, about 180 mm + 0.042 D(mm); many companies use a flat 300 mm minimum. Set the gas space above the high-high level to at least the larger of 0.2 D and 0.3 m, or 0.6 m with a mist eliminator. Find the length for the liquid, and the length for the droplets: L liq = (V H + V S ) / (A T − A V − A LLL ) L gas = (Q G /A V ) × (h V /U V ) (15) Take the larger length. Repeat with other diameters until L/D is between 1.5 and 6, and choose the lightest vessel that meets both. Svrcek and Monnery narrow the range by pressure: 1.5–3 up to 250 psig (about 17 barg), 3–4 from 250 to 500 psig (17–34 barg) and 4–6 above that. Typical horizontal two-phase separators end up with L/D of 3 to 5. 12 Low-pressure drums often end up shorter and fatter, because their walls are thin and the cost follows the shell area, not the wall thickness. Two more checks are worth making. The gas velocity over the liquid must stay low enough not to whip liquid off the surface; NORSOK’s typical maximum, 0.137 (L/6) 0.58 √[(ρ L − ρ G )/ρ G ], is a useful screen. 14 And the effective length available to the droplets is shorter than the shell: Campbell uses L e = L − D to allow for the inlet and outlet zones. 6 Effective length. The distance from the inlet device to the mist eliminator or gas outlet, not the tangent-to-tangent length. A cyclonic inlet or a perforated baffle makes more of the shell useful. Boots. When a small amount of water must also be removed from a hydrocarbon liquid, a boot under the drum keeps the interface level controllable without lengthening the drum. Figure 4. A correctly sized vessel with the wrong inlet will carry over. Excess momentum in the feed breaks liquid into fine mist that the mist eliminator cannot catch, and excess momentum in the gas outlet sucks gas through one part of the mist eliminator and leaves the rest idle. 37 Nozzles are therefore sized on momentum, ρv², rather than on velocity alone. None, or an open pipe end. Cheap, and prone to short-circuiting and jetting liquid onto the opposite wall. 12 Deflector or diverter plate. A flat or dished plate in front of the nozzle. It stops the jet but tends to make small droplets and foam. 12 Half-open pipe. A pipe stub with its lower half cut away, pointing the flow downward. A simple default for vertical drums with modest momentum. Vane inlet (Schoepentoeter and similar). Rows of curved vanes slice the feed sideways and spread the gas. It is the normal choice at moderate to high momentum for feeds that are mostly gas, and it copes with slugs. 8 Inlet cyclones. Use the feed momentum to spin out liquid, break foam and help coalescence, at momentums around ten times those of pipe inlets. 12 Give the inlet a straight run of about 5–10 pipe diameters with no pockets, so slugs and stratified flow arrive as evenly as possible. 38 ρv² is a pressure. 1 kg/(m·s²) = 1 Pa. It is twice the dynamic pressure, which is why vendors sometimes quote “dynamic pressure” limits half the size of a company’s ρv² limit. Check which one a figure is.

entries.h: Other internals worth naming on the data sheet
entries.x: Vortex breaker on every liquid outlet, usually crossed plates, to stop gas being drawn into the pump suction. 26 Mist eliminator drains. Liquid from a vane box or cyclone deck drains through a pipe that must be sealed below the lowest liquid level. The pressure drop across the device lifts liquid in the drain pipe; if the level is too high the device will not drain, and liquid can be siphoned. A small hole near the top of the drain pipe is sometimes used as a siphon breaker. 26 Perforated baffles or flow straighteners in horizontal drums to even out the gas and liquid velocity after the inlet. Sand jets and drains where solids arrive with the feed. Level bridles or chambers for the level instruments, with the trip transmitters on separate connections from the control transmitter. 09

entries.h: Vendor data and how to read it
entries.x: Most separator internals are bought, and most packaged separators are selected from a vendor’s range. Vendor data is good data, but it is quoted under the vendor’s conditions, which are rarely yours. Reading it well means finding the basis first and the number second.

entries.h: Mesh pad styles: four names for the same pad
entries.x: A mesh pad is described by four numbers: bulk density (kg/m³ of pad, which for stainless steel follows from the void fraction), void fraction, wire diameter and specific surface area (m² of wire per m³ of pad). Each vendor gives its styles its own names. Converting to the four numbers shows that the catalogues are much closer than the names suggest. Table 7. Roughly equivalent stainless-steel mesh styles. Imperial figures converted at 1 lb/ft³ = 16.02 kg/m³ and 1 ft²/ft³ = 3.281 m²/m³. Koch-Glitsch lists newer high-capacity styles replacing its traditional ones with more than 20 % more capacity at the same efficiency. 10 Class Density, kg/m³ Surface, m²/m³ Koch-Glitsch 10 Sulzer KnitMesh 8 AMACS 9 Okutani 11 High capacity, dirty service 80 145–158 931, now 708 4540 (80, 145) 7CA (80, 148) SK-80 (80, 158) Standard, general purpose 144 258–280 431, now 172 9030 (144, 258) 4CA (144, 279) SK-144 (144, 280) Heavy duty, higher efficiency 192 350–377 421, now 709 9033 (192, 350) 4BA (192, 377) SK-192 (192, 375) Fine wire, very high efficiency 115–192 390–660 326 (128 kg/m³, 0.15 mm wire) 36 9001 (192, 643) 3BF (115, 394), 3BA (192, 656) – Okutani lists its SK-80, SK-144 and SK-192 styles as equivalent to York (now Koch-Glitsch) 931, 431 and 421, which is a useful check on the table. 11 Standard wire is 0.011 in (0.28 mm) or 0.25 mm; fine wire is about 0.15 mm.

Vendor K-values are usually for air and water at ambient conditions: AMACS quotes 0.35 ft/s (0.107 m/s) for vertical flow and 0.42 ft/s for horizontal flow on that basis. 9 Sulzer’s standard KnitMesh is quoted at K up to 0.107 m/s, its V-MISTER at up to 0.13 m/s and its 9797 design at up to 0.12 m/s. 8 None of these numbers applies directly at 70 bar with a condensate. Derate for pressure (Table 1), liquid load and foaming, and ask the vendor to rate the device at your conditions and your liquid load. Density is not efficiency. A denser pad has more wire to hit, but it also floods earlier. The fine-wire styles get their efficiency from thinner wire, not just more of it. Figure 5.
