A grade efficiency curve gives the fraction of droplets of each size that the device removes, at one velocity, one pressure and one fluid pair. Read three numbers from it: the size removed at 50 %, at 90 % and at 99 %. Then check four things before you use them: The test fluid and pressure. Figure 5 shows why: the same pad loses most of its fine-droplet efficiency at high pressure, because the gas is denser, the droplets slow less and the velocity through the pad is far lower. The velocity. Efficiency for small droplets falls as velocity falls. At turndown the pad you bought may be a coarse filter. Move the velocity slider to 25 % to see it. The liquid load. Curves are usually for light loads. Above the load limit, capacity falls (section 05). The droplet size reaching the device. A curve that removes everything above 10 µm is no use if the inlet device is making 5 µm mist.

Pressure drop rises slowly with velocity until the device starts to load with liquid, then rises steeply near flooding. A clean, dry mesh pad is typically under 2.5 mbar, vane packs 1–10 mbar and cyclone decks up to about 30 mbar. 8 Two practical uses: a rising ΔP in operation means fouling or flooding, and the device ΔP sets how far liquid rises in its drain pipe, which in turn sets how far below the low-low level the drain must be sealed.

Packaged separators, such as well-test units, are sold from capacity tables. Table 8 reproduces two rows of SLB’s published table for its conventional horizontal test separators. 25 Table 8. Two rows from a published capacity table. Working pressure is at 38 °C; oil capacity is at 1 min retention. The sheet does not state the pressure, gas gravity or liquid density behind the gas figures. 25 Model Vessel size Working pressure, kPa Oil, high level, m³/d Oil, low level, m³/d Gas, high level, m³/d Gas, low level, m³/d SEP-C 42 in × 10 ft 9,928 2,289 1,057 708,000 1,698,000 SEPL-E 48 in × 18 ft 9,928 4,770 2,862 2,123,000 2,973,000 How to read it: One vessel, two operating points. “High” and “low” are liquid level settings. At high level the vessel holds more oil for its minute of retention and leaves less area for gas, so the oil rating rises and the gas rating falls. You choose the level, and you get one pair, not the best of both columns. Find the basis. Oil capacity is tied to 1 min of retention, the API 12J figure for light oil. If your oil is heavier or foams, your capacity is lower in proportion to the retention time you need. 5 Find what is missing. The gas figures are in standard volume, but the sheet does not say at what pressure. Gas capacity at a fixed velocity rises roughly in proportion to pressure, so a figure quoted at full working pressure means much less capacity at half the pressure. Ask. Check it independently. Example 9 backs out the liquid fill and the K-value the SEP-C rating implies. If a vendor figure implies a K well above the ranges in Table 2, ask what internals justify it.

entries.h: What to send, and what to check in the bid
entries.x: Send every operating case with gas and liquid rates, densities, viscosities, surface tension, molar mass, Z, and the liquid load and droplet distribution if you have them. Include turndown. State the inlet piping arrangement, expected slugs, foaming tendency, solids and wax. Ask for the K-value and the area it refers to, the predicted outlet liquid carryover (for example in US gal/MMscf or mg/Sm³), the pressure drop and the turndown, for each case. Check that the proposed vessel height leaves the spacings in Table 4, that the drain seals work at your level settings, and that the materials match the vessel’s corrosion and temperature basis. Carryover guarantees. Glycol contactor and compressor scrubber vendors often guarantee carryover in US gallons of liquid per million standard cubic feet of gas. Sulzer, for example, quotes 0.1 US gal/MMscf for one glycol contactor design. 8 A guarantee is only as good as the test method agreed with it. 10

Process design hands mechanical design a diameter, a height, nozzles, internals, a design pressure and temperature, a corrosion allowance and a material. Mechanical design returns wall thicknesses and a weight, and sometimes a reason to change the diameter. It is worth knowing the shell formulas well enough to check them.

Design pressure is set above the maximum operating pressure with enough margin for the relief valve to sit above normal fluctuations without simmering; Svrcek and Monnery’s example uses 110 % of operating pressure; 2 a common company rule is the greater of 110 % and operating plus 1.7 bar (25 psi), which governs on low-pressure drums. Design temperature covers the highest operating temperature plus a margin, and the minimum design metal temperature (MDMT) covers the coldest case, including auto-refrigeration during depressuring.

entries.h: Shell and head thickness to ASME VIII Division 1
entries.x: For internal pressure P, inside radius R and diameter D in the corroded condition, allowable stress S and joint efficiency E, the long-standing Division 1 formulas are: 17 Cylindrical shell, hoop stress (UG-27(c)(1)): t = P R / (S E − 0.6 P) (16) Cylindrical shell, longitudinal stress (UG-27(c)(2)): t = P R / (2 S E + 0.4 P) (17) 2:1 ellipsoidal head (UG-32(d)): t = P D / (2 S E − 0.2 P) Hemispherical head: t = P R / (2 S E − 0.2 P) (18) Valid for the hoop formula when P ≤ 0.385 S E and t ≤ R/2. Add the corrosion allowance and the plate under-tolerance, and allow for thinning when heads are formed. Rearranged, the same equations give the maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP) of the plate actually chosen, P = S E t / (R + 0.6 t) for the shell. The standard hydrostatic test pressure is 1.3 × MAWP × the ratio of allowable stress at test temperature to that at design temperature. 17 The most common carbon-steel plate for separators is SA-516 Grade 70, with an allowable stress of 20,000 psi (138 MPa) at moderate temperatures. 42 Check ASME Section II Part D at your design temperature, and the impact-test rules at your MDMT. Which edition? The 2025 edition of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code was released in July 2025 and became mandatory on 1 January 2026. 32 It reorganized parts of Division 1 and points several design rules to Division 2, so check paragraph numbers against the edition your project is contracted to. Joint efficiency. 1.0 with full radiography, 0.85 with spot radiography for typical butt welds. Table 9. Under Section VIII Division 1, a pressure relief system must keep the pressure from rising more than 10 % (or 20 kPa) above MAWP with a single device, 16 % with multiple devices, and 21 % in a fire. 17 The overpressure protection rules have since moved into ASME Section XIII. 18

Pressure vessels designed for more than 15 psig (103 kPa), apart from the small vessels the code exempts, must have their design registered with the provincial safety authority under CSA B51, which gives the design a Canadian Registration Number (CRN) that appears on the nameplate. In British Columbia the authority is Technical Safety BC. 19 The current edition of CSA B51 is the 2024 edition. 19 Plan for registration in the schedule: a vessel built elsewhere without a CRN cannot be installed until it has one.

A separator sits between a high-pressure source and lower-pressure equipment, holds a flammable inventory, and protects machines that cannot take liquid. API RP 14C’s safety analysis table for pressure vessels lists what can go wrong and the sensor that should catch it. 20 Table 11. Undesirable events and safety devices for a pressure vessel, after the API RP 14C safety analysis table. 20 PSH, PSL: high and low pressure sensors; LSH, LSL: high and low level sensors; TSH: high temperature sensor; PSV: pressure safety valve; FSV: check valve; ESS: emergency support systems. Event Causes Detectable condition Primary protection Further measures I would add Overpressure Blocked or restricted outlet, upstream control failure, gas blowby from an upstream vessel, fire High pressure PSH and PSV Size the PSV for every credible case; independent PAHH trip on the inlet ESD valve Liquid overflow Inflow above outflow, slugs, blocked liquid outlet, level control failure High liquid level LSH Independent LAHH trip of the feed or of the downstream compressor; enough surge time to act Gas blowby Liquid outflow above inflow, liquid outlet left open, level control failure Low liquid level LSL Independent LALL closing a shutdown valve on the liquid outlet; downstream PSV sized for blowby Leak Corrosion, erosion, impact, vibration Low pressure PSL and FSV Gas detection, corrosion monitoring, inspection to API 510 Excess temperature Heater or temperature control failure (heated vessels) High temperature TSH Shutdown of the heat source

API 521 estimates the heat absorbed by the wetted wall of a vessel in a pool fire as Q = 43,200 F A w 0.82 W, with adequate drainage and prompt firefighting (19) Q = 70,900 F A w 0.82 W, without them (20) A w is the wetted area in m², counted only up to 7.6 m (25 ft) above grade or the fire source; F is the environment factor, 1.0 for a bare vessel. 16 40 The relief rate is the heat input divided by the latent heat at relieving conditions, W = Q/λ. Near the critical point, where the latent heat is small, API 521 suggests a minimum of 115 kJ/kg as an approximation. 40 The gas-filled upper part of a vessel has no liquid to cool it; its wall can lose strength in a fire before the relief valve lifts, which is why depressuring systems exist alongside relief valves.

If an upstream separator loses its liquid level and its level control valve is open, gas at upstream pressure flows through a valve sized for liquid into a downstream vessel. When the upstream pressure exceeds the downstream vessel’s MAWP, this is often the largest relief case on the downstream drum. API 521 does not allow credit for a favourable control response, so the valve is assumed to stay where the failure left it, and the bypass valve may have to be assumed open as well. 31 41 The gas flow through the valve follows the control-valve sizing equation of IEC 60534-2-1: 21 W = N 6 C v Y √(x p 1 ρ 1 ), Y = 1 − x/(3 F γ x T ), x ≤ F γ x T , F γ = k/1.40 (21) W in kg/h with N 6 = 27.3 for p 1 in bar absolute and ρ 1 in kg/m³; x = Δp/p 1 ; x T is the valve’s pressure-differential ratio factor. When x reaches F γ x T the flow is choked and Y = 2/3. The remedies are to size the downstream relief valve for the blowby flow, to limit the valve trim or add a restriction orifice so the blowby flow is smaller without affecting normal liquid flow, or to provide an independent low-low level trip, which some companies accept as a high-integrity protection system in place of relief capacity. 41

Liquid reaching a compressor, a turbine fuel system or a flare can destroy equipment or start a fire. The defences are a conservative K for the service, an inlet device matched to the inlet momentum, a mist eliminator that works across the whole flow range, and an independent high-high level trip with enough surge volume between LAH and LAHH for the trip to act before liquid reaches the inlet nozzle.

Low temperature. Depressuring a vessel, or flashing liquid across its drain valve, can chill steel below its MDMT. Check auto-refrigeration cases and choose impact-tested steel where needed. Hydrates and ice in drains, level bridles and instrument connections: heat tracing, insulation, methanol or glycol injection, and drains that can be cleared safely. Sour service. H₂S is toxic and causes sulfide stress cracking: select materials to NACE MR0175/ISO 15156. Iron sulfide deposits can be pyrophoric when a vessel is opened, so keep them wet and purge with nitrogen. Erosion from sand at the inlet nozzle and the opposite wall: wear plates, inlet devices, and velocities below the erosional limit. Foaming that carries liquid into the gas outlet: a lower K, antifoam, or a cyclonic inlet. Draining to atmosphere. Never drain a pressurized separator to an open drain through a single valve; liquid flashes, the valve can freeze open, and gas follows the liquid. Vessel entry. Separators are confined spaces with residual hydrocarbons, H₂S and nitrogen. Isolation, purging, gas testing and an entry permit come before anyone goes through the manway.

What is the highest pressure any upstream source can impose, and can the vessel see it? What is the blowby flow if the upstream level valve and its bypass fail open? How long between LAH and LAHH, and between LAHH and the inlet nozzle, at the maximum liquid rate? Are the trip transmitters independent of the control transmitter, and tested? What is the coldest the steel can get during depressuring? Where does the liquid go when the drain is opened, and what does it do when it flashes? The 7.6 m rule. Only the wetted area within 7.6 m of the base of a pool fire is counted, because experience has shown that sizing on the average heat input up to that height is enough. 40 Blowby is two-phase first. The upstream vessel’s liquid arrives before its gas. The downstream relief valve can see liquid, then two-phase flow, then gas. 31 12

Examples 1 to 8 follow one stream from a flash calculation through a vertical inlet separator, its nozzles, wall thickness and relief loads, to the low-pressure flash drum it feeds. Example 9 reads a vendor’s capacity table. All numbers were checked in code; small differences in the last digit are rounding.

Given 1,000 kmol/h of feed at 40.0 bar absolute and 15 °C: methane 0.60, ethane 0.10, propane 0.10, n-butane 0.08, n-pentane 0.07, n-hexane 0.05 (mole fractions). K from the Wilson correlation, equation (3). Find The vapour fraction, the phase compositions and the mass flows of each phase. Wilson K-values with T c , p c and ω from standard tables: C1 7.245 C2 0.857 C3 0.184 nC4 0.044 nC5 0.012 nC6 0.004 Check for two phases. At β = 0 the Rachford–Rice sum is Σz(K−1) = +3.456; at β = 1 it is Σz(K−1)/K = −20.87. One sign change, so there is one root between 0 and 1. Solve equation (1) by bisection or Newton’s method: β = V/F = 0.6554 Compositions from equation (2): Component z K x (liquid) y (vapour) Methane 0.60 7.245 0.1178 0.8535 Ethane 0.10 0.857 0.1104 0.0946 Propane 0.10 0.184 0.2150 0.0395 n-Butane 0.08 0.044 0.2141 0.0095 n-Pentane 0.07 0.012 0.1986 0.0024 n-Hexane 0.05 0.004 0.1441 0.0005 Flows and molar masses: V = 655.4 kmol/h, M_V = 19.05 kg/kmol → 12,485 kg/h of gas L = 344.6 kmol/h, M_L = 53.88 kg/kmol → 18,565 kg/h of liquid Two-thirds of the moles leave as gas, but 60 % of the mass leaves as liquid. The separator sees a modest gas flow and a large liquid flow, which Example 3 will show is a liquid-controlled vessel. Round to 12,500 kg/h of gas and 18,600 kg/h of liquid for the examples that follow.

entries.h: Example 2. Terminal velocity of a 150 µm droplet
entries.x: Given Gas from Example 1 at 40.0 bar a and 15 °C with Z = 0.90; liquid density 620 kg/m³; gas viscosity 0.012 mPa·s. Find The terminal velocity of a 150 µm droplet and the K it corresponds to. Gas density, equation (9): ρ_G = 40.0e5 × 19.05 / (0.90 × 8,314 × 288.15) = 35.3 kg/m³ Start with Stokes’ law and check Re: v = 9.81 × (150e-6)² × (620 − 35.3) / (18 × 1.2e-5) = 0.598 m/s Re = 35.3 × 0.598 × 150e-6 / 1.2e-5 = 264 → far outside Stokes’ range Iterate equations (5) and (6): Re 264 → C_D 0.715 → v 0.213 Re 94.1 → C_D 1.132 → v 0.169 Re 74.8 → C_D 1.269 → v 0.160 Re 70.7 → C_D 1.306 → v 0.158 converged: v_t = 0.157 m/s, Re = 69.3, C_D = 1.32 Equivalent K, equation (7): K = 0.157 / √((620 − 35.3)/35.3) = 0.157 / 4.07 = 0.0386 m/s check: √(4 × 9.81 × 150e-6 / (3 × 1.32)) = 0.0386 m/s Stokes’ law would have overestimated the velocity almost four times. And a gravity-only K of 0.0386 m/s is below the GPSA no-mist-eliminator value of 0.047 m/s at this pressure, which corresponds to about 180 µm. Figure 3 reproduces these numbers.

entries.h: Example 3. A vertical inlet separator where the liquid controls
entries.x: Given 12,500 kg/h of gas (ρ G 35.3 kg/m³) and 18,600 kg/h of liquid (ρ L 620 kg/m³, so 30.0 m³/h) at 39 barg. Standard mesh pad, half-open-pipe inlet, holdup 5 min, surge 2.5 min. Find Diameter, height, level settings and mist-eliminator size. Actual gas flow and K: Q_G = 12,500 / 3,600 / 35.3 = 0.0983 m³/s K = 0.107 − 0.003 × (39 − 7)/7 = 0.0933 m/s (Table 1) V_max = 0.0933 × 4.07 = 0.380 m/s Diameter from the gas: D_ME = √(4 × 0.0983 / (π × 0.380)) = 0.574 m D = 0.574 + 0.10 = 0.674 → round up to 0.75 m Liquid heights at 0.75 m: A = 0.442 m², Q_L = 0.500 m³/min h_H = 5 × 0.500 / 0.442 = 5.66 m, h_S = 2.83 m → H/D ≈ 14 A 14:1 vessel is not sensible. The liquid controls. Widen in 150 mm steps until H/D ≤ 4. At D = 1.20 m, H/D = 4.25; at D = 1.35 m: A = 1.431 m², h_H = 1.747 m, h_S = 0.873 m bottom to LALL 0.300 LAHH to inlet ℄ 0.300 + 0.203/2 = 0.401 inlet ℄ to pad = max(0.5 × 1.35, 0.61 + 0.101) = 0.711 pad 0.150 pad to top tangent = max(0.15, (1.35 − 0.154)/2 − 1.35/4) = 0.260 H_TT = 0.300 + 1.747 + 0.873 + 0.401 + 0.711 + 0.150 + 0.260 = 4.443 → 4.5 m, H/D = 3.3 Check the mesh pad: full-diameter pad: v = 0.0983 / 1.431 = 0.069 m/s = 18 % of V_max → below turndown 650 mm pad in a box: v = 0.0983 / 0.332 = 0.296 m/s = 78 % of V_max Level settings above the bottom tangent: LALL 300 NLL 2,047 LAHH 2,920 inlet ℄ 3,321 pad 4,033–4,183 mm 30 s of liquid = 0.00833 × 30 / 1.431 = 0.175 m (> 100 mm), so LAL ≈ 475 mm and LAH ≈ 2,745 mm by the NORSOK spacing Gas alone would fit in a 0.75 m drum; the liquid needs 1.35 m. Widening the vessel then left a full-diameter mesh pad running at 18 % of design, where it would barely work, so the pad is sized for the gas and boxed in. With this much liquid, a horizontal drum is worth pricing too. Select the Example 3 preset in Figure 1 to see the same vessel drawn to scale.

entries.h: Example 4. A horizontal low-pressure flash drum
entries.x: Given Downstream flash drum at 5.0 bar a (4 barg) and 40 °C: 6,000 kg/h of gas with M = 28, Z = 0.98; 90 m³/h of liquid at 650 kg/m³. No mist eliminator. Holdup 10 min, surge 5 min. Find Diameter and length, and the level settings. Gas properties and settling velocity: ρ_G = 5.0e5 × 28 / (0.98 × 8,314 × 313.15) = 5.49 kg/m³, Q_G = 0.304 m³/s K = 0.107/2 = 0.0535 m/s (below 7 barg, no pressure derating) U_T = 0.0535 × √((650 − 5.49)/5.49) = 0.580 m/s, U_V = 0.75 U_T = 0.435 m/s Volumes and a first diameter, equation (14) with L/D = 4: V_H = 10 × 90/60 = 15.0 m³, V_S = 7.5 m³ D = [4 × 22.5 / (0.6 × π × 4)]^(1/3) = 2.29 m For D = 2.4 m: A_T = 4.524 m² LLL = 300 mm (Svrcek’s 0.5 D(ft) + 7 in gives 278 mm): h/D = 0.125, A_LLL = 0.326 m² h_V = max(0.2 × 2.4, 0.30) = 0.48 m: A_V = f(0.2) × A_T = 0.1424 × 4.524 = 0.644 m² L_liq = 22.5 / (4.524 − 0.644 − 0.326) = 6.33 m → 6.5 m L_gas = (0.304/0.644) × (0.48/0.435) = 0.472 × 1.10 = 0.52 m The liquid controls by a wide margin. Compare diameters: D 2.1 m → L 8.5 m, L/D 4.0, shell + heads 65.6 m² D 2.4 m → L 6.5 m, L/D 2.7, shell + heads 61.5 m² D 2.7 m → L 5.0 m, L/D 1.9, shell + heads 58.2 m² At 4 barg the walls are thin, so area tracks cost. Choose 2.4 × 6.5 m: an L/D of 2.7 is inside the 1.5–3 range Svrcek and Monnery give below about 17 barg, without being stubby. Levels on the chosen drum, from equation (13): NLL: A = 0.326 + 15.0/6.5 = 2.634 m² → h = 1,355 mm LAHH: A = 2.634 + 7.5/6.5 = 3.788 m² → h = 1,873 mm; gas space 527 mm at LAHH: gas velocity 0.413 m/s, droplet falls 0.527 m in 1.21 s, travelling 0.50 m NORSOK screen: 0.137 × 10.84 × ((6.5 − 2.4)/6)^0.58 = 1.19 m/s ≫ 0.41 m/s A design droplet reaches the liquid within half a metre of the inlet, so the gas section is far bigger than it needs to be: this drum is a liquid surge vessel with a gas outlet. The Figure 4 calculator opens on this case.

entries.h: Example 5. Nozzles for the vertical separator
entries.x: Given The Example 3 flows, a half-open-pipe inlet, and Table 5 limits. Schedule 40 pipe inside diameters. Find Inlet, gas outlet and liquid outlet nozzle sizes. Feed mixture: Q_m = 12,500/35.3 + 18,600/620 = 354.1 + 30.0 = 384.1 m³/h = 0.1067 m³/s ρ_m = 31,100 / 384.1 = 81.0 kg/m³ Inlet, ρv² ≤ 2,100 Pa: v ≤ √(2,100/81.0) = 5.09 m/s → d ≥ √(4 × 0.1067/(π × 5.09)) = 0.163 m NPS 8 (ID 202.7 mm): v = 3.30 m/s, ρv² = 884 Pa Gas outlet, ρv² ≤ 3,750 Pa: v ≤ √(3,750/35.3) = 10.3 m/s → d ≥ 0.110 m NPS 6 (ID 154.1 mm): v = 5.27 m/s, ρv² = 981 Pa Liquid outlet, v ≤ 1 m/s: Q_L = 0.00833 m³/s → d ≥ 0.103 m NPS 4 (ID 102.3 mm) gives 1.01 m/s, just over; NPS 6 gives 0.45 m/s Take NPS 6 with a vortex breaker. Erosional velocity of the inlet line, API RP 14E with C = 100: ρ_m = 81.0 kg/m³ = 5.06 lb/ft³ → v_e = 100/√5.06 = 44.5 ft/s = 13.6 m/s ≫ 3.3 m/s The inlet came out well under its momentum limit because the next size down, NPS 6, would give 5.7 m/s and about 2,650 Pa, over the limit. Always check the size you pick, not just the minimum.

entries.h: Example 6. Shell and head thickness to ASME VIII Division 1
entries.x: Given The Example 3 vessel, 1,350 mm inside diameter, maximum operating pressure 39.0 barg. Design pressure 110 % of operating. SA-516-70, S = 138 MPa at design temperature; full radiography, E = 1.0; corrosion allowance 3 mm; 2:1 ellipsoidal heads. Find Shell and head thickness, the MAWP of the chosen shell plate, and the hydrotest pressure. Design pressure: P = 1.1 × 39.0 = 42.9 barg = 4.29 MPa Shell, equation (16), radius in the corroded condition: R = 675 + 3 = 678 mm t = 4.29 × 678 / (138 × 1.0 − 0.6 × 4.29) = 2,909 / 135.4 = 21.5 mm plus corrosion allowance: 24.5 mm → order 26 mm plate checks: P = 4.29 ≤ 0.385 SE = 53.1 MPa; t ≤ R/2 Head, equation (18): t = 4.29 × 1,356 / (2 × 138 − 0.2 × 4.29) = 21.1 mm, plus 3 mm = 24.1 mm order 28 mm plate to allow for thinning when the head is formed MAWP of the 26 mm shell, corroded thickness 23 mm: P = 138 × 23 / (678 + 0.6 × 23) = 4.59 MPa = 45.9 barg Hydrotest at 1.3 × MAWP × stress ratio, taking the stress ratio as 1.0: nameplate MAWP 42.9 barg → test 55.8 barg nameplate MAWP 45.9 barg → test 59.6 barg Rounding up the plate gave 7 % more pressure capacity than asked for. Stamping the vessel at the higher MAWP costs nothing now and can save a re-rating later, but it raises the test pressure and must agree with the relief valve set pressure.

Given The Example 3 vessel on a skirt with its bottom tangent 1.2 m above grade, bare, with adequate drainage and firefighting. Wetted to LAHH (2.92 m above the bottom tangent), a conservative choice. Latent heat at relieving conditions taken as 280 kJ/kg. Find Heat input and relief rate. Height check: top of wetted zone = 1.2 + 2.92 = 4.12 m < 7.6 m → all of it counts Wetted area: 2:1 head ≈ 1.084 D² = 1.084 × 1.35² = 1.98 m² shell = π × 1.35 × 2.92 = 12.38 m² A_w = 14.36 m² Heat input, equation (19): Q = 43,200 × 1.0 × 14.36^0.82 = 43,200 × 8.89 = 384 kW Relief rate: W = 384,000 / 280,000 × 3,600 = 4,940 kg/h without drainage, equation (20): Q = 630 kW, W = 8,100 kg/h The fire case is real but not large for this vessel. A blocked gas outlet with the upstream source still feeding would ask the valve to pass the full 12,500 kg/h of gas plus any vapour from the liquid, so fire is unlikely to set the orifice. It must still be documented, and it is the one case allowed 21 % accumulation instead of 10 %.

entries.h: Example 8. Gas blowby into the low-pressure drum
entries.x: Given The Example 3 separator sends its liquid to the Example 4 drum through a level control valve with C v = 25 and x T = 0.70. The downstream drum has a 10 barg design pressure and its relief valve relieves at 11 barg (12.0 bar a). Upstream gas: 40.0 bar a, 35.3 kg/m³, k = 1.27. Find The blowby gas flow if the separator loses its level with the valve fully open. Pressure ratio and choking, equation (21): x = (40.0 − 12.0)/40.0 = 0.700 F_γ = 1.27/1.40 = 0.907, F_γ x_T = 0.635 → x > 0.635, choked x = 0.635, Y = 1 − 0.635/(3 × 0.635) = 0.667 Flow: W = 27.3 × 25 × 0.667 × √(0.635 × 40.0 × 35.3) = 455 × 29.9 = 13,600 kg/h Is the valve too big? The normal liquid duty, before allowing for flashing, needs only K_v = Q √(SG/Δp) = 30.0 × √(0.62/35) = 4.0, C_v = 1.156 K_v = 4.6 A valve with C v = 10, still twice the normal requirement, would cut the blowby to 13,600 × 10/25 = 5,450 kg/h. The blowby flow is more than twice the downstream drum’s normal gas flow of 6,000 kg/h, so it is likely to set that drum’s relief valve. The cheapest safeguard is often the one in step 3: do not oversize the level valve. An independent low-low level trip closing a shutdown valve is the other common answer.

entries.h: Example 9. Reading a packaged separator capacity table
entries.x: Given The SEP-C row in Table 8: 42 in × 10 ft, 9,928 kPa working pressure; oil 2,289 m³/d at high level and 1,057 m³/d at low level for 1 min retention; gas 708,000 and 1,698,000 m³/d. Assume an inside diameter of 0.98 m, a 3.048 m shell, heads ignored, gas relative density 0.65 with Z = 0.85 at 38 °C, oil 800 kg/m³. Find The liquid fill behind each rating, and the K the gas ratings imply if they are quoted at full working pressure. Shell volume: A = π × 0.98²/4 = 0.754 m², V = 0.754 × 3.048 = 2.30 m³ One minute of oil: high level: 2,289/1,440 = 1.590 m³ → 69 % of the shell (h/D ≈ 0.65) low level: 1,057/1,440 = 0.734 m³ → 32 % of the shell (h/D ≈ 0.36) Gas mass flow and actual volume at full working pressure: standard density = 0.65 × 1.223 = 0.795 kg/m³ low level: 1,698,000 × 0.795 / 86,400 = 15.6 kg/s ρ_G = 100.3e5 × 18.8 / (0.85 × 8,314 × 311.15) = 85.9 kg/m³ → Q = 0.182 m³/s Velocity and implied K: low level: gas area 0.68 × 0.754 = 0.513 m² → v = 0.355 m/s K = 0.355 / √((800 − 85.9)/85.9) = 0.123 m/s (0.40 ft/s) high level: gas area 0.233 m², v = 0.326 m/s, K = 0.113 m/s Consistency: the gas ratings differ by a factor of 2.40 and the gas areas by 2.21, so the two columns describe one vessel at two levels. Read this way, the table is coherent: K of about 0.11–0.12 m/s is at or just below the bottom of API 12J’s horizontal range (0.122–0.152 m/s for a 3 m vessel). But that range is not derated for pressure the way GPSA’s mesh-pad values are, and at 99 barg a derated figure would be lower. The question to send the vendor is the one the sheet leaves open: at what pressure, gas density and liquid density are the gas ratings quoted, and with which internals? 13
Work each one before opening the solution. Answers are accepted within 2 % unless stated. Use g = 9.81 m/s² and R = 8,314 J/(kmol·K).

A vertical knockout drum with a mesh pad receives 2.0 m³/s of gas at actual conditions. Gas density 18 kg/m³, liquid density 700 kg/m³. Using K = 0.10 m/s, find the minimum mist-eliminator diameter. Diameter m V_max = 0.10 × √((700 − 18)/18) = 0.616 m/s A = 2.0 / 0.616 = 3.25 m², D = √(4 × 3.25/π) = 2.03 m The vessel itself would be 2.25 m after the support-ring allowance and rounding up in 150 mm steps.

What K does the GPSA rule give for a vertical drum with a horizontal mesh pad at 56 barg? K m/s K = 0.107 − 0.003 × (56 − 7)/7 = 0.107 − 0.021 = 0.086 m/s That is 20 % below the low-pressure value, on top of the density effect already in the Souders–Brown equation.

Find the density of a natural gas with M = 18.5 kg/kmol and Z = 0.86 at 70 bar absolute and 30 °C. Density kg/m³ ρ = 70e5 × 18.5 / (0.86 × 8,314 × 303.15) = 59.7 kg/m³ Using Z = 1 would understate the density by 14 % and oversize the vessel’s velocity limit.

A vertical drum of 1.5 m inside diameter receives 30 m³/h of liquid. The specification asks for 8 min of holdup and 4 min of surge. What height is needed between LALL and LAHH? Height m A = π × 1.5²/4 = 1.767 m², Q_L = 0.5 m³/min h_H = 8 × 0.5/1.767 = 2.26 m, h_S = 4 × 0.5/1.767 = 1.13 m, total 3.40 m With the fixed spacings this vessel will be over 5 m tall, H/D above 3.5: a candidate for a horizontal comparison.

entries.h: Problem 5. Stokes’ law, and whether it applies
entries.x: Find the Stokes terminal velocity of a 50 µm water droplet (998 kg/m³) in air at 20 °C (1.20 kg/m³, 0.0181 mPa·s). Is Stokes’ law valid here? Velocity m/s v = 9.81 × (50e-6)² × (998 − 1.2) / (18 × 1.81e-5) = 0.0750 m/s Re = 1.20 × 0.0750 × 50e-6 / 1.81e-5 = 0.25 Re is well below 1, so Stokes applies. The full correlation, equation (6), gives 0.070 m/s, 6 % lower, because even at Re = 0.25 the inertial term adds a little drag.

What fraction of a horizontal drum’s cross-section lies below a liquid level at one quarter of the diameter? Fraction – θ = 2 arccos(1 − 2 × 0.25) = 2 arccos(0.5) = 2.094 rad f = (2.094 − sin 2.094)/(2π) = (2.094 − 0.866)/6.283 = 0.196 By symmetry, a level at three quarters of the diameter leaves the same fraction, 0.196, for the gas.

A feed of 0.50 m³/s with a mean density of 45 kg/m³ enters through a vane-type inlet device limited to ρv² = 8,000 Pa. Find the minimum nozzle inside diameter. What would it be with no inlet device, limited to 1,400 Pa? Diameter, vane inlet m vane inlet: v = √(8,000/45) = 13.3 m/s → d = √(4 × 0.50/(π × 13.3)) = 0.219 m no device: v = √(1,400/45) = 5.58 m/s → d = 0.338 m The inlet device lets the nozzle be a size or two smaller than the line, and more important, protects the droplet size distribution.

Find the required shell thickness, including corrosion allowance, for a separator with design pressure 2.0 MPa, inside diameter 2,000 mm, SA-516-70 at 138 MPa, spot radiography (E = 0.85) and a 3 mm corrosion allowance. Thickness mm R = 1,000 + 3 = 1,003 mm t = 2.0 × 1,003 / (138 × 0.85 − 0.6 × 2.0) = 2,006 / 116.1 = 17.3 mm plus CA: 20.3 mm → order 22 mm Full radiography (E = 1.0) would save about 3 mm of steel over the whole shell.

A bare vessel with adequate drainage and firefighting has 25 m² of wetted area below 7.6 m. The latent heat at relieving conditions is 300 kJ/kg. Find the relief rate. Relief rate kg/h Q = 43,200 × 25^0.82 = 43,200 × 14.0 = 605 kW W = 605,000 / 300,000 × 3,600 = 7,260 kg/h Doubling the wetted area raises the load by only 2^0.82 = 1.77 times.

A scrubber’s mesh pad is designed for 30,000 kg/h of gas at its design K. If the pad works down to 25 % of its design velocity, what is the lowest gas flow at the same pressure and temperature at which it still separates well? Gas flow kg/h At constant density, velocity ∝ mass flow: 0.25 × 30,000 = 7,500 kg/h If start-up or early-life flows are lower, a two-stage mist eliminator or a smaller boxed pad is the usual answer.

A feed of 40 mol % light component (K = 3.2) and 60 mol % heavy component (K = 0.45) is flashed. Find the vapour fraction V/F. V/F – 0.40 × 2.2/(1 + 2.2β) − 0.60 × 0.55/(1 − 0.55β) = 0 0.88(1 − 0.55β) = 0.33(1 + 2.2β) → 0.55 = 1.21β → β = 0.455 With two components Rachford–Rice reduces to a linear equation; with more, it needs iteration.

An existing vertical scrubber of 1.2 m inside diameter with a full-diameter mesh pad now handles 0.55 m³/s of gas at actual conditions, 50 barg, ρ G = 30 kg/m³, ρ L = 600 kg/m³. What K is it running at? Compare it with the GPSA value at this pressure. Operating K m/s V = 0.55 / (π × 1.2²/4) = 0.486 m/s K = 0.486 / √((600 − 30)/30) = 0.112 m/s GPSA at 50 barg: 0.107 − 0.003 × 43/7 = 0.0886 m/s → 26 % over Before replacing the vessel, ask a vendor to rate a high-capacity mesh, a mesh-and-vane combination or a cyclone deck in the existing shell.

A level control valve with C v = 40 and x T = 0.72 fails open on a separator at 30 bar a. Gas density upstream 25 kg/m³, k = 1.30. The downstream vessel relieves at 6 bar a. Find the blowby gas flow. Gas flow kg/h x = (30 − 6)/30 = 0.80; F_γ = 1.30/1.40 = 0.929; F_γ x_T = 0.669 → choked x = 0.669, Y = 2/3 W = 27.3 × 40 × 0.667 × √(0.669 × 30 × 25) = 728 × 22.4 = 16,300 kg/h Once the flow is choked, lowering the downstream pressure further adds nothing; raising the upstream pressure adds in proportion.

A vessel has an MAWP of 25 barg at a design temperature where the allowable stress is 118 MPa. At test temperature the allowable stress is 138 MPa. What is the standard hydrostatic test pressure? Test pressure barg 1.3 × 25 × 138/118 = 38.0 barg The stress ratio raises the test for hot vessels, so that the test loads the steel as hard as the design condition does.

entries.h: Problem 15. Settling length in a horizontal drum
entries.x: In a horizontal drum the gas space above LAHH is 0.9 m deep. The design droplet falls at 0.20 m/s and the gas moves at 0.8 m/s. What is the minimum effective length? Length m fall time = 0.9/0.20 = 4.5 s; L = 0.8 × 4.5 = 3.6 m Add the inlet and outlet zones: with Campbell’s L − D allowance, a 2 m drum would need about 5.6 m tangent to tangent.

entries.h: Problem 16. What a vendor rating implies
entries.x: A packaged horizontal separator of 0.98 m inside diameter and 3.048 m shell length is rated at 2,289 m³/d of oil with 1 min retention. Ignoring the heads, what fraction of the shell volume is liquid at that rating? Fraction – 1 min of oil = 2,289/1,440 = 1.590 m³ shell = π × 0.98²/4 × 3.048 = 2.299 m³ → 0.69 About 69 % full, so the high-level rating leaves less than a third of the cross-section for gas. That is why its gas rating is lower. 14

entries.h: What goes on the separator data sheet
entries.x: The data sheet is where process design becomes a purchase. Everything a vendor needs to size, rate and guarantee the separator should be on it, for every operating case. Service and cases. Tag, service, and every case: normal, maximum, minimum, start-up, upset, end of life. Gas. Mass flow, molar mass, Z, density, viscosity at separator conditions. Liquid. Mass and volume flow, density, viscosity, surface tension; a second liquid phase if present. Conditions. Operating pressure and temperature; design pressure, design temperature and MDMT; vacuum design if needed. Feed character. Flow regime in the inlet line, slug volume and frequency, solids, wax, foaming tendency, H₂S, CO₂, chlorides. Performance. Allowable liquid carryover in the gas (US gal/MMscf or mg/Sm³) and gas carry-under in the liquid. Liquid volumes. Holdup and surge times with their definitions; LALL, LAL, NLL, LAH and LAHH as heights and times. Internals. Inlet device, mist eliminator type and material, vortex breakers, baffles, sand jetting, drain arrangements. Nozzles. Schedule of sizes, flange classes and facings, services and orientations; manways. Instruments. Level control and independent trip connections, bridles, pressure and temperature connections. Relief. Relief valve set pressure and the governing case, with the fire and blowby cases noted. Materials and construction. Material, corrosion allowance, sour service, post-weld heat treatment, insulation and heat tracing. Codes. ASME VIII Division 1 (or the contract code), CSA B51 registration where the vessel is installed in Canada, API RP 12J and the owner’s standards. Layout. Orientation, plot limits, elevation needed for the pump NPSH, skid or transport limits. 15
